title: NHA Phlebotomy Technician (CPT)
blurb: The National Healthcareer Association CPT exam: 100 scored items plus 20 unscored pretest items in two hours, across safety and compliance, patient preparation, routine and special collections, and processing. Each attempt here draws 100 by the real domain weights.

questions.q: Under standard precautions, how should a phlebotomist treat a patient's blood and body fluids?
choices: As infectious only if the patient has a known diagnosis
As infectious only if visible blood is present
As potentially infectious regardless of the patient's diagnosis
As infectious only when an isolation sign is posted
questions.why: Standard precautions assume all blood, body fluids, secretions, and non-intact skin are potentially infectious for every patient. Waiting for a known diagnosis or an isolation sign fails, because most infected patients are undiagnosed at the time of the draw.

questions.q: A phlebotomist collects specimens from a patient with confirmed Clostridioides difficile infection. What hand hygiene is required after removing gloves?
choices: Soap and water handwashing, because alcohol does not kill C. difficile spores
Alcohol-based hand rub, because it is faster and equally effective
No hand hygiene, because gloves were worn the entire time
Alcohol rub followed by donning a second pair of gloves
questions.why: C. difficile forms spores that alcohol-based rubs do not kill; the friction of soap-and-water washing physically removes them. The alcohol rub choice is tempting because it is the routine default, but it is specifically inadequate for spore formers.

questions.q: How long should a phlebotomist rub hands together with soap and water during routine handwashing?
choices: At least 5 seconds
At least 10 seconds
At least 60 seconds
At least 20 seconds
questions.why: CDC guidance specifies at least 20 seconds of vigorous scrubbing with soap and water. Ten seconds is a common misremembering and is not long enough to adequately remove transient flora.

questions.q: Which is the correct order for donning personal protective equipment before entering an isolation room?
choices: Gloves, gown, mask, goggles
Gown, mask or respirator, goggles or face shield, gloves
Mask, gloves, gown, goggles
Goggles, gloves, gown, mask
questions.why: Donning goes gown, then mask or respirator, then eye protection, then gloves last so the glove cuffs cover the gown sleeves. Putting gloves on first is wrong because they would then be contaminated while adjusting the other items.

questions.q: Which item is removed FIRST when doffing PPE after a blood draw in a contact precautions room?
choices: Mask or respirator
Goggles
Gloves
Gown
questions.why: Gloves are removed first because they are the most contaminated item; the mask or respirator is removed last, after leaving the room, since it protects the airway until exit. Removing the mask first would expose the face while the hands are still soiled.

questions.q: Immediately after withdrawing the needle from a patient's vein, what should the phlebotomist do with the safety device?
choices: Activate the safety feature before disposing of the needle in the sharps container
Recap the needle using the one-hand scoop technique, then discard it
Set the needle on the tray until the bandage is applied
Remove the needle from the holder and discard the needle alone
questions.why: Engineered sharps injury protection must be activated immediately at the point of use, before disposal. Recapping, even one-handed, is not the standard for a device with a built-in safety feature and adds an unnecessary injury opportunity.

questions.q: A sharps container in a drawing station is three-quarters full. What is the correct action?
choices: Press the contents down to make room
Continue using it until the contents reach the lid
Close and replace it when it reaches the fill line, about two-thirds to three-quarters full
Pour the contents into a red biohazard bag
questions.why: Sharps containers are sealed and replaced at the manufacturer's fill line, typically two-thirds to three-quarters full, to prevent overfilling and protrusion injuries. Never push contents down or transfer them, as both actions put hands near exposed sharps.

questions.q: A phlebotomist sustains a needlestick from a used needle. What is the FIRST action?
choices: Report the injury to the supervisor
Wash the site with soap and running water
Request the source patient's HIV test result
Complete an incident report form
questions.why: The immediate first step is decontaminating the wound by washing with soap and running water; reporting and evaluation follow. Reporting is required but is not first, since delay in cleansing increases inoculum exposure.

questions.q: The OSHA Bloodborne Pathogens Standard is found at which citation?
questions.why: 29 CFR 1910.1030 is the Bloodborne Pathogens Standard. 29 CFR 1910.1200 is the Hazard Communication Standard covering chemicals and SDS, which is a related but different rule.

questions.q: How often must an employer review and update the written exposure control plan?
choices: At least annually and whenever new tasks or procedures affect exposure
Every three years
Only after a documented exposure incident
Only when OSHA conducts an inspection
questions.why: The standard requires review and update at least annually and whenever changes in tasks, procedures, or positions alter occupational exposure. Waiting for an exposure incident or an inspection is reactive and not compliant.

questions.q: Which statement about the hepatitis B vaccination is correct for a newly hired phlebotomist?
choices: The employee must pay a share of the cost
It must be offered at no cost within 10 working days of initial assignment
It is mandatory and cannot be refused
It may be offered only after a documented exposure
questions.why: The employer must offer the vaccine series free of charge within 10 working days of initial assignment to work with exposure risk. The employee may decline, but must sign the OSHA declination form, so calling it mandatory is incorrect.

questions.q: A phlebotomist declines the hepatitis B vaccine. What must happen?
choices: The employee is reassigned to non-exposure duties
The employee forfeits the vaccine permanently
The employee signs a declination form and may still receive the vaccine later at no cost
No documentation is needed if the refusal is verbal
questions.why: A signed OSHA declination form is required, and the employee retains the right to free vaccination at any later date while still covered. Treating the refusal as permanent misstates the standard.

questions.q: Which item belongs in a red biohazard bag rather than regular trash?
choices: A blood-saturated gauze pad
An empty specimen bag with no visible contamination
A paper requisition form
An unused alcohol prep pad wrapper
questions.why: Items saturated or dripping with blood are regulated medical waste and require a biohazard bag. A clean, uncontaminated specimen bag is not regulated waste and overfilling biohazard streams needlessly raises disposal cost.

questions.q: What must appear on a container of regulated medical waste?
choices: The collecting phlebotomist's name and license number
The patient's name and date of birth
The biohazard symbol with fluorescent orange or orange-red background
A green recycling symbol
questions.why: OSHA requires the biohazard legend and symbol on a fluorescent orange or orange-red background, or the use of red bags or containers. Patient identifiers must never appear on waste containers, as that would expose PHI.

questions.q: A tube of blood breaks on the floor. After absorbing the spill and removing glass with forceps, what disinfectant concentration is appropriate?
choices: 1:100 dilution of household bleach
70 percent isopropyl alcohol
Plain soap and water
1:10 dilution of household bleach
questions.why: A 1:10 bleach dilution, roughly 5000 ppm available chlorine, is the standard for blood spill decontamination. A 1:100 dilution is used for routine surface cleaning of non-porous surfaces without gross blood, and alcohol is not appropriate for a blood spill.

questions.q: Where should a phlebotomist look to find the flash point and first aid measures for a chemical used in the lab?
choices: The Safety Data Sheet for that chemical
The laboratory procedure manual
The exposure control plan
The Joint Commission standards manual
questions.why: Safety Data Sheets contain a standardized 16 sections covering hazards, handling, first aid, and physical properties such as flash point. The exposure control plan addresses bloodborne pathogens, not chemical properties.

questions.q: On an NFPA 704 diamond, what does the blue quadrant indicate?
choices: Flammability
Health hazard
Reactivity or instability
Special hazards such as oxidizer
questions.why: Blue is health, red is flammability, yellow is reactivity, and white is special hazards. Red and blue are frequently swapped by test takers, so anchor on blue equals health.

questions.q: What does the acronym RACE stand for in hospital fire response?
choices: Report, Alert, Contain, Escape
Remove, Alarm, Contain or Confine, Extinguish or Evacuate
Respond, Assess, Call, Evacuate
Rescue, Assess, Close, Exit
questions.why: RACE is Rescue or Remove people in danger, Alarm, Contain or Confine the fire by closing doors, then Extinguish or Evacuate. Rescuing people always precedes attempting to extinguish, which is why options that lead with assessing or calling are wrong.

questions.q: A small electrical fire starts in a centrifuge. Which extinguisher class is appropriate?
choices: Class A
Class B
Class D
Class C
questions.why: Class C extinguishers are rated for energized electrical equipment. Class A is for ordinary combustibles such as paper and would use water, which conducts electricity and creates a shock hazard.

questions.q: Using the PASS technique, what does the second S represent?
choices: Sweep the nozzle side to side at the base of the fire
Shut the door behind you
Stand six feet back
Signal for assistance
questions.why: PASS is Pull the pin, Aim at the base of the fire, Squeeze the handle, Sweep side to side. Aiming at the flames rather than the base, or confusing the step with signaling, will fail to smother the fuel source.

questions.q: A phlebotomist notices a frayed cord on a blood collection cart's power strip. What is the correct action?
choices: Wrap the cord in electrical tape and continue using it
Remove the equipment from service, tag it, and report it to maintenance
Use it only for low-draw devices
Unplug it at the end of the shift and report it next week
questions.why: Damaged electrical equipment must be taken out of service and reported immediately, because a frayed cord is both a shock and a fire hazard. Field repairs with tape are not acceptable and leave the hazard in place.

questions.q: A phlebotomist must draw a patient in the radiology suite during an active imaging procedure. Which principle minimizes radiation exposure?
choices: Wear a surgical mask and double gloves
Face the radiation source at all times
Maximize distance, minimize time, and use shielding
Stand directly behind the imaging tube
questions.why: Time, distance, and shielding are the three cardinal principles of radiation protection. PPE for infection control offers no protection from ionizing radiation, which is why the mask and gloves option is a distractor.

questions.q: A patient is on airborne precautions for suspected tuberculosis. What respiratory protection does the phlebotomist need?
choices: A fit-tested N95 respirator or higher
A standard surgical mask
A face shield alone
No respiratory protection if the draw takes under five minutes
questions.why: Airborne precautions require a fit-tested N95 or higher-level respirator because droplet nuclei stay suspended and travel on air currents. A surgical mask is adequate for droplet precautions such as influenza, but does not seal or filter to the N95 level.

questions.q: Which precaution category is correct for a patient with suspected pertussis?
choices: Airborne precautions with a negative-pressure room
Droplet precautions with a surgical mask within three to six feet
Contact precautions only
Standard precautions only
questions.why: Pertussis spreads by large respiratory droplets that travel only about three to six feet, so droplet precautions with a surgical mask apply. Airborne precautions and negative pressure are reserved for tuberculosis, measles, and varicella.

questions.q: In the chain of infection, a contaminated tourniquet reused between patients best represents which link?
choices: Reservoir
Portal of entry
Mode of transmission
Susceptible host
questions.why: The tourniquet acts as a vehicle carrying organisms from one person to another, which is the mode of transmission link. The reservoir is where the pathogen normally lives and multiplies, not the object that merely carries it.

questions.q: Which practice reflects correct body mechanics when a phlebotomist lifts a heavy box of supplies?
choices: Bend at the waist and lift with the back
Twist at the waist while lifting to save a step
Hold the load away from the body for better visibility
Bend the knees, keep the back straight, and hold the load close to the body
questions.why: Squatting with a straight back and keeping the load close uses the strong leg muscles and reduces lumbar strain. Twisting while loaded is a common cause of back injury and should be replaced by pivoting with the feet.

questions.q: A patient reports a latex allergy before a venipuncture. What is the appropriate response?
choices: Use nitrile gloves and a latex-free tourniquet and bandage
Use latex gloves but wash hands first
Use powdered latex gloves to reduce contact
Proceed normally, since a brief contact is harmless
questions.why: All latex-containing items in the encounter, including the tourniquet and bandage, must be replaced with latex-free alternatives. Powdered latex gloves are actually worse, because the powder aerosolizes latex protein.

questions.q: Which organization or regulation governs all laboratory testing performed on human specimens in the United States for the purpose of diagnosis?
choices: The Joint Commission
CLSI
CLIA
CDC
questions.why: CLIA is the federal regulation establishing quality standards for all non-research human laboratory testing. CLSI writes consensus standards and guidelines such as GP41 for venipuncture, but those are voluntary rather than regulatory.

questions.q: Running a normal and abnormal control on a glucose meter before testing patient samples is an example of what?
choices: Quality assurance
Quality control
Proficiency testing
A delta check
questions.why: Quality control is the measurable testing of known materials to verify the analytic system is working. Quality assurance is the broader program covering the whole pre-analytic, analytic, and post-analytic process, of which QC is one component.

questions.q: A phlebotomist mislabels a tube and the error is caught before testing. What should happen?
choices: Correct the label quietly and say nothing, since no harm occurred
Document the event on an incident or occurrence report and notify the supervisor
Note the error only in the patient's chart
Discard the tube and take no further action
questions.why: Near misses are reported on an incident report so trends can be tracked and processes improved. Silently correcting the label hides data from the quality assurance program, even though the patient was not harmed.

questions.q: A coworker asks about a celebrity patient whose blood the phlebotomist just drew. Under HIPAA, what is the correct response?
choices: Share the information because the coworker is also an employee
Share only the diagnosis, not the name
Share the information if the coworker promises confidentiality
Decline, because the coworker has no treatment-related need to know
questions.why: HIPAA allows disclosure only to those with a legitimate treatment, payment, or operations need, under the minimum necessary standard. Being an employee does not by itself create a need to know.

questions.q: Which action best demonstrates the HIPAA minimum necessary standard?
choices: Accessing only the requisition information required to perform the assigned draw
Reviewing the full chart to better understand the patient
Printing the complete medical record to carry on rounds
Discussing the case in the elevator with another technician
questions.why: Minimum necessary limits access and disclosure to the smallest amount of PHI needed for the task. Reading the full chart out of curiosity exceeds what the draw requires, even when the intent is benign.

questions.q: A competent adult inpatient says no when the phlebotomist approaches to draw blood. What should the phlebotomist do?
choices: Proceed, because the physician ordered the test
Ask a nurse to hold the patient's arm
Stop, document the refusal, and notify the nurse or provider
Wait ten minutes and attempt the draw while the patient sleeps
questions.why: A competent patient has the right to refuse, and proceeding over that refusal could constitute battery. A physician order authorizes the test but does not override the patient's consent.

questions.q: A phlebotomist raises a needle toward a patient who has said no and the patient reasonably fears being stuck. Which term describes this act?
choices: Negligence
Assault
Battery
Res ipsa loquitur
questions.why: Assault is the threat or apprehension of harmful contact; battery is the actual unconsented touching. The distinction matters because the needle has not yet touched the patient in this scenario.

questions.q: A patient asks the phlebotomist what an elevated potassium result means for her health. What is the appropriate response within scope of practice?
choices: Explain the general clinical significance of high potassium
Tell the patient the result is probably nothing to worry about
Refer the patient to her provider, who will interpret and discuss the results
Look up the reference range and read it aloud to reassure her
questions.why: Interpreting laboratory results is outside a phlebotomist's scope of practice and belongs to the ordering provider. Offering reassurance that the value is harmless is equally out of scope and could delay needed care.

questions.q: A phlebotomist enters an outpatient drawing station and calls the next name on the list. Which set of identifiers meets the two-identifier requirement?
choices: Room number and bed assignment
Physical appearance and the name on the requisition
Full name and date of birth stated by the patient
The name the patient answers to when called from the waiting room
questions.why: Two independent identifiers such as full name and date of birth, stated by the patient and matched to the requisition, are required. Calling a name and accepting a nod is not acceptable because patients with hearing loss or similar names commonly answer to the wrong name.

questions.q: An unconscious trauma patient arrives in the emergency department with no identification. How should the phlebotomist identify the patient before the draw?
choices: Use the temporary identification number assigned by the facility and attached to the patient
Wait until a family member arrives to give a name
Label the tubes as unknown male and add a name later
Ask the paramedic to state a name from the scene
questions.why: Facilities assign a temporary or John or Jane Doe number that is banded to the patient and used on the requisition and labels. Waiting for family delays emergent testing and is not required once the temporary number exists.

questions.q: A phlebotomist is drawing an inpatient. The armband is not on the patient but is taped to the bedside table. What is the correct action?
choices: Use the armband on the table since it is the correct patient
Ask the patient to hold the band while identifying
Draw the patient and ask nursing to reband afterward
Have the nurse reband the patient before the draw
questions.why: An inpatient armband is only valid while attached to the patient; a loose band must be replaced by nursing before collection. Using the band from the table is a common identification error because it cannot be tied to the person in the bed.

questions.q: Which element is NOT required on a laboratory requisition?
choices: Ordering provider name
Phlebotomist home address
Tests requested
Patient full name and date of birth
questions.why: Requisitions require patient identifiers, ordering provider, tests requested, date and time, and any special instructions. The collector's personal address is never part of the requisition, although the collector's initials or ID go on the tube label.

questions.q: A phlebotomist notices that a basic metabolic panel appears twice on the same patient for the same collection time. What should be done?
choices: Contact the nursing unit or laboratory to verify whether the duplicate order is intended before collecting
Draw two separate sets to satisfy both orders
Cancel one order independently and collect once
Collect once and discard the second requisition
questions.why: Duplicate orders are verified with the unit or laboratory so the patient is not drawn twice unnecessarily. The phlebotomist does not have the authority to cancel a physician order on their own.

questions.q: Which statement best reflects proper introduction technique at the bedside?
choices: Enter quietly and begin assembling supplies without speaking
Introduce yourself only if the patient asks who you are
State your name, your department, and explain that you are there to collect a blood sample
Tell the patient the draw will not hurt at all
questions.why: A proper introduction includes the collector's name, department, and purpose of the visit, which reduces anxiety and supports consent. Promising that it will not hurt is false reassurance and destroys trust when the needle is inserted.

questions.q: A competent adult extends her arm and rolls up her sleeve after the phlebotomist explains the venipuncture. This is an example of which type of consent?
choices: Informed consent
Implied consent
Expressed written consent
Surrogate consent
questions.why: Implied consent is demonstrated by the patient's cooperative actions rather than words. Informed consent involves a documented discussion of risks, benefits, and alternatives and is typically required for more invasive procedures.

questions.q: An alert inpatient states that he does not want his blood drawn. What should the phlebotomist do?
choices: Draw the sample because the physician ordered it
Ask a family member to convince the patient
Return in one hour and attempt the draw without asking
Stop, document the refusal, and notify the nurse or ordering provider
questions.why: A competent patient has the right to refuse; proceeding anyway could constitute battery. The refusal must be documented and communicated so the care team can follow up rather than simply being retried without discussion.

questions.q: Which approach is most appropriate when preparing to draw blood from a 4-year-old child?
choices: Tell the child the needle will not be used
Explain the full procedure 30 minutes in advance to prepare the child
Use simple honest language, keep the explanation brief, and allow a parent to help comfort the child
Ask the parent to restrain the child alone in the hallway
questions.why: Short, honest, age-appropriate explanations with a parent providing comfort work best for preschoolers. Long advance explanations increase anticipatory anxiety in young children.

questions.q: An elderly patient with thin, fragile skin and poor vein elasticity is scheduled for a routine draw. Which modification is most appropriate?
choices: Apply the tourniquet loosely or use a blood pressure cuff at low pressure and anchor the vein carefully
Apply the tourniquet very tightly to distend the vein
Use a 16 gauge needle to speed collection
Slap the antecubital area briskly to raise the vein
questions.why: Fragile skin and veins call for reduced tourniquet pressure and careful anchoring to prevent bruising and vein rolling. A tight tourniquet increases the risk of skin tears and hematoma in geriatric patients.

questions.q: A patient tells the phlebotomist that she fainted during her last blood draw. What is the best preparation step?
choices: Draw the blood quickly while the patient stands
Have the patient hold her breath during the draw
Withhold the draw until a physician is present
Place the patient in a supine or reclined position before beginning
questions.why: A history of syncope calls for reclining the patient so a faint does not result in a fall injury. Drawing a fainting-prone patient while standing is the highest risk position.

questions.q: A patient scheduled for a lipid panel asks how long she must fast. What is the standard instruction?
choices: 4 to 6 hours with no water
9 to 12 hours with water permitted
2 hours with clear liquids permitted
24 hours with nothing by mouth
questions.why: Lipid panels traditionally require a 9 to 12 hour fast, and water is allowed and encouraged to prevent dehydration. Withholding water is incorrect because dehydration hemoconcentrates the specimen.

questions.q: A fasting blood glucose is ordered. Which fasting interval is standard?
choices: 8 to 10 hours
1 to 2 hours
16 to 20 hours
No fasting is needed
questions.why: Fasting blood glucose generally requires 8 to 10 hours without food. Prolonged fasting beyond about 12 hours is not recommended because it can alter results and stress the patient.

questions.q: Which best defines the basal state?
choices: Any time the patient has not eaten for 4 hours
The condition immediately after moderate exercise
The resting metabolic state early in the morning after about 12 hours of fasting and no strenuous activity
The state of the patient during an active infection
questions.why: Basal state refers to a resting, fasting condition roughly 12 hours after the last intake, typically obtained in the early morning before activity. A short 4-hour fast does not produce basal conditions.

questions.q: A patient smoked a cigarette 10 minutes before arriving for a draw. Which effect is most likely?
choices: Decreased hemoglobin
Elevated white blood cell count and cortisol
Decreased glucose
No measurable effect on any analyte
questions.why: Smoking transiently raises WBC count, cortisol, and glucose among other analytes. It does not lower hemoglobin; chronic smoking actually tends to raise hemoglobin and hematocrit.

questions.q: A patient reports finishing an intense workout 20 minutes ago. Which action is most appropriate?
choices: Proceed with the draw with no comment
Cancel the test permanently
Have the patient drink a sports beverage first
Allow the patient to rest and note the recent exercise for the laboratory
questions.why: Strenuous exercise elevates creatine kinase, lactate, and potassium, so rest before collection and documentation of the activity are appropriate. Giving a sports beverage would further alter glucose and electrolytes.

questions.q: A serum cortisol is ordered and no collection time is specified. Why does timing matter?
choices: Cortisol is unaffected by time of day
Cortisol is highest at midnight
Cortisol shows diurnal variation and peaks in the early morning, around 0800
Cortisol can only be drawn while fasting
questions.why: Cortisol follows a diurnal rhythm with a peak around 0800 and a trough late in the evening, so collection time must be recorded. Midnight represents the low point, not the peak.

questions.q: Which analyte also demonstrates diurnal variation, typically running higher in the morning?
choices: Serum iron
Serum albumin
Total protein
Chloride
questions.why: Serum iron is highest in the morning and drops later in the day, so timed collection matters. Albumin and total protein vary mainly with posture and hydration rather than a daily rhythm.

questions.q: A trough level for vancomycin should be collected at which time?
choices: 30 minutes after the infusion ends
Immediately before the next scheduled dose
Midway between two doses
Any time convenient for the unit
questions.why: A trough reflects the lowest concentration and is drawn immediately before the next dose. A sample taken 30 minutes after an infusion would approximate a peak, not a trough.

questions.q: A peak drug level is ordered for an intramuscular antibiotic. When is it generally drawn?
choices: Immediately before the dose is given
12 hours after the dose
At the same time as the trough
About 30 minutes to 1 hour after administration, per protocol
questions.why: Peak levels are collected after absorption is complete, commonly about 30 to 60 minutes after an IM dose depending on the drug and facility protocol. Drawing before the dose yields a trough.

questions.q: Which instruction is correct for a patient scheduled for a 2-hour oral glucose tolerance test?
choices: Fast 8 to 12 hours beforehand, then drink the entire glucose solution within 5 minutes
Eat a low carbohydrate breakfast before arriving
Sip the glucose solution slowly over 1 hour
Chew gum during the test to reduce nausea
questions.why: The GTT requires a fast of 8 to 12 hours and the glucose load is consumed within about 5 minutes, with timing started at the last swallow. Gum stimulates digestion and can alter glucose results.

questions.q: During a glucose tolerance test the patient vomits 15 minutes after drinking the solution. What should the phlebotomist do?
choices: Give a second dose of glucose and restart
Continue and note the vomiting on the final tube only
Notify the provider or laboratory because the test may need to be rescheduled
Shorten the test to 1 hour
questions.why: Vomiting invalidates the glucose load, so the provider or laboratory decides whether to stop and reschedule. The phlebotomist cannot redose the patient on their own authority.

questions.q: A patient scheduled for a fasting lipid panel admits to drinking coffee with cream 2 hours ago. What is the best action?
choices: Proceed and say nothing
Wait 30 minutes and then draw
Have the patient drink water and draw immediately
Notify the provider or laboratory and reschedule or note the nonfasting status
questions.why: Coffee with cream breaks the fast and affects triglycerides, so the nonfasting status must be reported and the draw rescheduled or flagged. Waiting 30 minutes does not restore a fasting state.

questions.q: Which beverage is generally permitted during a fast?
choices: Black coffee
Plain water
Unsweetened tea
Diet soda
questions.why: Only plain water is permitted during a fast, and it helps prevent hemoconcentration. Black coffee is not allowed because caffeine alters several analytes even without calories.

questions.q: A visibly anxious adult patient states he has a strong fear of needles. Which action is best?
choices: Tell him to stop worrying because it is quick
Show him the needle to prove it is small
Speak calmly, recline him, and use distraction while working efficiently
Have him stand so he can leave quickly if needed
questions.why: Calm communication, a reclined position, and distraction lower the risk of a vasovagal response in needle-phobic patients. Displaying the needle typically escalates anxiety.

questions.q: A seated patient becomes pale and diaphoretic during a draw. What is the first action?
choices: Remove the tourniquet and needle, then lower the patient's head and apply a cold compress
Finish filling the remaining tubes quickly
Leave the patient to get help
Give the patient juice immediately while upright
questions.why: The draw must be terminated immediately and the patient protected from a fall, with the head lowered and a cold compress applied. Leaving a syncopal patient unattended risks an unwitnessed fall injury.

questions.q: A patient had a left-sided mastectomy with lymph node removal 3 months ago. Which arm should be used?
choices: Left arm, because the surgery is healed
Right arm, avoiding the side of the mastectomy
Either arm at the phlebotomist's discretion
Neither arm; only a finger stick is allowed
questions.why: Draws are avoided on the side of a mastectomy with lymph node dissection because of lymphostasis and infection risk, so the unaffected side is used. A 3-month interval does not remove the restriction; provider approval is required for the affected side.

questions.q: A patient has an IV running in the left forearm and no accessible veins in the right arm. What is the preferred approach?
choices: Draw directly above the running IV
Draw from the IV line without stopping the infusion
Draw from the IV site itself
Draw below the IV after the nurse has stopped the infusion for 2 minutes, and document it
questions.why: If no alternative site exists, collection is made distal to the site after the infusion is stopped for about 2 minutes, with a discard volume and documentation. Drawing above a running IV contaminates the specimen with infusing fluid.

questions.q: The only accessible antecubital area shows a large purple hematoma. What should the phlebotomist do?
choices: Select a different vein distal to the hematoma or use the other arm
Draw through the hematoma since the vein is visible
Massage the hematoma to disperse it, then draw
Apply the tourniquet directly over the hematoma
questions.why: Blood drawn through a hematoma is contaminated with hemolyzed extravascular blood and gives erroneous results, so another site is chosen. Massaging a hematoma causes pain and further tissue damage.

questions.q: Why should venipuncture be avoided in an edematous arm?
choices: Edema makes the skin too tough to penetrate
Edema increases clotting factors in the sample
Excess tissue fluid alters test results and the site heals poorly
Edema makes veins bleed excessively
questions.why: Edematous tissue contains excess interstitial fluid that dilutes and contaminates the specimen, and the compromised tissue heals poorly. Edema does not raise clotting factors in the drawn sample.

questions.q: A patient has extensive scarring from burns across both antecubital areas. Which action is most appropriate?
choices: Draw through the scar tissue using a larger gauge needle
Select an alternative site such as a hand vein away from the scarred and burned tissue
Apply heat to the scars to soften them
Refuse to collect the sample
questions.why: Scarred and burned skin is difficult to penetrate, painful, and prone to infection, so an unaffected site such as a hand vein is used. Refusing to collect is unnecessary when alternative sites exist.

questions.q: A patient has a cast on the right arm and a dialysis fistula in the left forearm. What should the phlebotomist do?
choices: Draw from the fistula since it has excellent flow
Draw from the arm with the cast above the cast edge
Use a capillary stick on a toe
Look for an acceptable vein such as a hand vein on the fistula arm only with provider approval, or consult the nurse
questions.why: A fistula or graft is never used or compressed by a phlebotomist, and a casted limb is avoided, so the nurse or provider must direct the alternative. Puncturing a fistula risks clotting and loss of the access.

questions.q: A patient requests the draw be taken through a large forearm tattoo. What is the best response?
choices: Proceed because tattoo ink does not affect specimens
Use the tattoo only if it is older than 1 year
Choose a vein outside the tattooed area whenever possible
Cleanse the tattoo twice and proceed
questions.why: Tattooed skin may be more prone to infection, can obscure vein visualization, and dye may interfere, so an untattooed site is preferred. Extra cleansing does not resolve these issues.

questions.q: The intended site has active dermatitis with open, weeping skin. What is the correct action?
choices: Select a different site away from the affected skin
Cleanse with extra alcohol and proceed
Cover the rash with gauze and puncture through it
Use povidone-iodine instead of alcohol and proceed
questions.why: Compromised skin should not be punctured because of infection risk to both patient and collector, so another site is chosen. Changing the antiseptic does not make damaged skin an acceptable puncture site.

questions.q: Where should a tourniquet be applied, and for how long?
choices: Directly over the antecubital fossa for 3 minutes
6 to 8 inches above the site for 2 minutes
At the wrist for 1 minute
3 to 4 inches above the intended site for no more than 1 minute
questions.why: Standard practice is 3 to 4 inches proximal to the site with a maximum of 1 minute to avoid hemoconcentration. Leaving it on 2 to 3 minutes falsely elevates analytes such as potassium and total protein.

questions.q: A phlebotomist has spent 90 seconds locating a vein with the tourniquet on. What should be done?
choices: Continue searching since the vein is almost found
Release the tourniquet, wait 2 minutes, then reapply
Tighten the tourniquet to improve filling
Have the patient pump the fist vigorously
questions.why: If the tourniquet has been on longer than 1 minute it is released and reapplied after about 2 minutes to let circulation normalize. Vigorous fist pumping falsely raises potassium.

questions.q: Which characteristic best identifies a suitable vein on palpation?
choices: Bouncy and resilient with a defined path
Hard and cordlike
Pulsating with each heartbeat
Flat and nonpalpable but clearly visible
questions.why: A good vein feels bouncy and resilient and can be traced. A pulsating vessel is an artery and a hard cordlike vessel is likely sclerosed or thrombosed.

questions.q: In the H-shaped antecubital vein pattern, which vein is the first choice?
choices: Basilic vein
Cephalic vein
Median cubital vein
Brachial vein
questions.why: The median cubital vein is the first choice because it is large, well anchored, and farthest from the brachial artery and median nerve. The basilic vein is a last resort for exactly the opposite reasons.

questions.q: In the M-shaped antecubital pattern, which vein is generally selected first?
choices: Median basilic vein
Median cephalic vein
Basilic vein
Accessory cephalic vein
questions.why: In the M pattern the median cephalic, on the lateral or thumb side, is the preferred first choice. The median basilic lies medially near the brachial artery and median nerve and is chosen last.

questions.q: Why is the basilic vein the last choice for venipuncture?
choices: It is too superficial to enter
It collapses under any tourniquet pressure
It is always thrombosed
It lies close to the brachial artery and median nerve
questions.why: The basilic vein's proximity to the brachial artery and median nerve makes accidental arterial puncture and nerve injury more likely. It is not inherently thrombosed or too superficial.

questions.q: A phlebotomist decides to use a dorsal hand vein. Which preparation change is appropriate?
choices: Use a 16 gauge needle and a large evacuated tube
Apply the tourniquet at the elbow only
Use a winged infusion set with a smaller gauge needle and anchor the vein firmly
Insert at a 45 degree angle
questions.why: Hand veins are small and mobile, so a winged set with a 23 gauge needle and firm anchoring is standard. A large bore needle with high vacuum is likely to collapse the vein.

questions.q: A patient's veins are difficult to locate. Which warming technique is appropriate?
choices: Apply a warm compress at about 42 degrees Celsius for 3 to 5 minutes
Immerse the arm in hot water for 15 minutes
Use a heating pad on the highest setting for 10 minutes
Rub the site briskly with alcohol until warm
questions.why: Warming at approximately 42 degrees Celsius for 3 to 5 minutes increases blood flow safely. Higher temperatures or prolonged application risk burns, especially in infants and the elderly.

questions.q: Why should a phlebotomist avoid slapping the antecubital area to raise a vein?
choices: It leaves a visible mark that confuses site selection
It causes hemolysis and petechiae and is painful and unprofessional
It permanently damages the median nerve
It causes arterial spasm and loss of pulse
questions.why: Slapping bruises tissue, can hemolyze blood, and is unprofessional; gentle massage upward from the wrist is the alternative. It does not cause permanent nerve damage or loss of pulse.

questions.q: Which statement about vigorous fist pumping before a draw is correct?
choices: It is required to fill the vein adequately
It has no effect on any laboratory value
It is recommended for all chemistry draws
It should be avoided because it falsely elevates potassium and ionized calcium
questions.why: Muscle activity releases potassium from cells and alters ionized calcium and lactate, so the patient makes a fist without pumping. A single closed fist is acceptable; repeated pumping is not.

questions.q: What is the correct technique for cleansing a routine venipuncture site?
choices: Cleanse with 70% isopropyl alcohol in concentric circles or a back-and-forth motion and allow it to air dry for 30 seconds
Cleanse with alcohol and blot dry with gauze immediately
Cleanse with sterile water and dry with gauze
Cleanse with alcohol and fan the site dry with your hand
questions.why: 70% isopropyl alcohol must be allowed to air dry about 30 seconds to be effective and to prevent stinging and specimen hemolysis. Blotting or fanning recontaminates the site and cuts the contact time short.

questions.q: A phlebotomist re-palpates the cleansed site immediately before inserting the needle. What must be done?
choices: Nothing, the glove keeps the site sterile
Wipe the glove with alcohol only
Cleanse the site again with 70% alcohol and allow it to dry
Insert the needle quickly to limit contamination
questions.why: Touching the prepared site recontaminates it, so it must be recleansed and allowed to dry. Gloves are not sterile, so glove contact does not preserve the prepared site.

questions.q: Which antiseptic is appropriate for skin preparation before collecting blood cultures on an adult?
choices: 70% isopropyl alcohol alone
Chlorhexidine gluconate
Sterile saline
Hydrogen peroxide
questions.why: Chlorhexidine gluconate is the standard blood culture skin prep for adults and patients over 2 months. Alcohol alone does not provide sufficient residual antisepsis to prevent contaminated cultures.

questions.q: Blood cultures are ordered on a 6-week-old infant. Which antiseptic is generally preferred?
choices: Chlorhexidine gluconate
Benzalkonium chloride
Povidone-iodine
Alcohol only, followed by drying
questions.why: Povidone-iodine is commonly used for infants under 2 months because chlorhexidine is not recommended for that age group. Alcohol alone remains inadequate for culture collection at any age.

questions.q: A blood alcohol level is ordered for a legal case. Which site prep is correct?
choices: 70% isopropyl alcohol
Ethyl alcohol swab
Tincture of iodine
A nonalcohol antiseptic such as benzalkonium chloride or soap and water
questions.why: Alcohol-based antiseptics can contaminate the specimen and are challenged in court, so a nonalcohol antiseptic is required. Isopropyl alcohol is not acceptable even though it is not the alcohol being measured.

questions.q: While preparing the tray, the phlebotomist notices that a box of evacuated tubes expired last month. What should be done?
choices: Remove the expired tubes from service and obtain unexpired tubes
Use them only for chemistry tests
Use them if the vacuum still draws blood
Use them and note the expiration on the requisition
questions.why: Expired tubes may have lost vacuum and degraded additives, producing inaccurate results, so they are removed from use. Successfully drawing blood does not prove that the additive is still effective.

questions.q: Which needle gauge is most appropriate for a routine adult antecubital venipuncture with an evacuated tube system?
choices: 16 gauge
21 or 22 gauge
25 gauge
18 gauge
questions.why: A 21 gauge is the standard multisample needle, with 22 gauge used for smaller veins. A 25 gauge is used for capillary or very small veins and increases hemolysis risk with vacuum draws.

questions.q: A patient speaks only Spanish and the phlebotomist speaks only English. What is the best action before the draw?
choices: Use hand gestures and proceed
Ask the patient's 8-year-old child to interpret
Obtain a qualified interpreter or facility language service before explaining the procedure
Skip the explanation since the procedure is routine
questions.why: A qualified interpreter or language line ensures accurate explanation and valid consent. Using a minor child as an interpreter is not acceptable practice.

questions.q: A patient who is hard of hearing is scheduled for a draw. Which technique is most effective?
choices: Face the patient, speak clearly at a moderate pace, and confirm understanding
Shout from the doorway
Speak only to the accompanying family member
Write nothing and rely on gestures alone
questions.why: Facing the patient at a moderate pace supports lip reading and comprehension, and understanding is confirmed. Shouting distorts speech and bypassing the patient to address family is disrespectful and risks identification errors.

questions.q: Before entering an airborne isolation room to draw blood, what should the phlebotomist do?
choices: Bring the entire phlebotomy tray into the room for convenience
Put on gloves only
Enter first and don PPE at the bedside
Take only the needed supplies and don the required PPE, including a fit-tested respirator, before entering
questions.why: Only necessary supplies enter an isolation room, and all required PPE including an N95 respirator is donned before entry. Bringing the full tray in risks contaminating equipment used on other patients.

questions.q: Which information should be confirmed and documented before the needle is inserted?
choices: The patient's insurance carrier
Patient identification, test orders, fasting status, and any site restrictions or allergies
The results of the previous week's tests
The patient's next scheduled appointment
questions.why: Identification, orders, fasting status, and site or allergy restrictions such as latex must be verified before the puncture. Insurance and appointment details are clerical and do not affect specimen integrity or patient safety.

questions.q: A phlebotomist must collect a blood culture, a CBC, a PT/INR, and a basic metabolic panel on an SST. Which tube is drawn first?
choices: Light blue sodium citrate
Gold SST
Blood culture bottle
Lavender EDTA
questions.why: Blood cultures are always first in the CLSI order of draw to minimize the chance of contaminating the sterile culture medium with skin flora or tube additives. The light blue tube is first among the additive tubes but still comes after cultures.

questions.q: Why does the light blue sodium citrate tube precede the gold SST in the order of draw?
choices: Clot activator or gel carryover into the citrate tube would alter coagulation results
Citrate tubes require a larger vacuum than SST tubes
SST tubes must always be drawn last in any order
Citrate evaporates if the tube sits in the rack
questions.why: Silica clot activator carried over from a serum tube into a citrate tube would falsely shorten clotting times, so citrate goes first among additive tubes. SST is not drawn last; gray oxalate/fluoride tubes come after it.

questions.q: A lavender EDTA tube is drawn before a gray sodium fluoride tube because carryover of which additive would most affect results?
choices: Silica into the fluoride tube
Thrombin into the EDTA tube
Citrate into the serum tube
Potassium EDTA into the glucose tube, elevating potassium and inhibiting some enzymes
questions.why: EDTA carryover raises potassium and chelates calcium needed by some assays, which is why EDTA is placed near the end and gray tubes last. Silica carryover is a concern for coagulation tubes, not fluoride tubes.

questions.q: Sodium fluoride in a gray-top tube functions primarily as which of the following?
choices: Anticoagulant that chelates calcium
Antiglycolytic agent that preserves glucose
Clot activator
Thrombin inhibitor
questions.why: Sodium fluoride inhibits glycolytic enzymes so glucose is not consumed by cells in the tube; the potassium oxalate paired with it is the anticoagulant that chelates calcium. Fluoride itself does not clot or activate clotting.

questions.q: Heparin prevents clotting by which mechanism?
choices: Binding calcium ions irreversibly
Precipitating calcium as an insoluble salt
Accelerating antithrombin III, which inhibits thrombin and factor Xa
Blocking platelet adhesion to glass
questions.why: Heparin works through antithrombin III to neutralize thrombin, so no calcium is removed and the plasma remains suitable for most chemistry tests. Calcium binding describes EDTA and citrate, not heparin.

questions.q: A provider orders a CBC with differential. Which tube should be collected?
choices: Light blue sodium citrate
Lavender EDTA
Green sodium heparin
Gray potassium oxalate/sodium fluoride
questions.why: EDTA preserves cell morphology and prevents platelet clumping, making it the tube of choice for CBC. Heparin distorts the white cell picture on a stained smear and is not acceptable for a differential.

questions.q: A light blue citrate tube is filled only about two-thirds full. What is the most likely effect on the PT/INR?
choices: Falsely prolonged results because excess citrate binds reagent calcium
Falsely shortened results from premature clotting
No effect as long as the tube is inverted
Hemolysis that invalidates only the platelet count
questions.why: The 9:1 blood-to-citrate ratio is required; a short draw leaves relatively too much citrate, which binds the calcium added during testing and falsely prolongs PT and PTT. The tube must be recollected, not simply re-inverted.

questions.q: The correct blood-to-anticoagulant ratio for a sodium citrate coagulation tube is:
questions.why: CLSI specifies 9 parts blood to 1 part 3.2 percent sodium citrate. Reversing the ratio to 1:9 would describe far more anticoagulant than blood and is not used for routine coagulation testing.

questions.q: How many inversions does an EDTA lavender tube typically require immediately after collection?
choices: 8 to 10
3 to 4
questions.why: EDTA tubes need 8 to 10 gentle inversions to fully mix the additive and prevent microclots. The 3 to 4 inversion figure applies to sodium citrate tubes, not EDTA.

questions.q: A nontube-additive red glass tube requires how many inversions?
choices: 8 to 10
5 to 6
3 to 4
questions.why: A plain red tube with no additive requires no inversions because there is nothing to mix. SST gold tubes with clot activator do require 5 inversions, which is the common point of confusion.

questions.q: Which needle gauge is considered standard for routine adult venipuncture with an evacuated tube system?
choices: 16 gauge
18 gauge
25 gauge
21 gauge
questions.why: A 21 gauge needle balances adequate flow with patient comfort and is the routine choice. The 16 to 18 gauge range is reserved for blood donor collection, where larger volume and unit integrity matter.

questions.q: A phlebotomist selects a winged infusion (butterfly) set for a patient with small hand veins. Which gauge is most appropriate?
choices: 23 gauge
16 gauge
18 gauge
14 gauge
questions.why: Butterfly sets are commonly 23 gauge, which fits small or fragile veins while still limiting hemolysis. Anything 18 gauge or larger is a donor or infusion size and would not enter a small hand vein safely.

questions.q: The needle should be inserted with the bevel up at what angle to the skin for routine venipuncture?
choices: 45 to 60 degrees
5 degrees or less
15 to 30 degrees
90 degrees
questions.why: A 15 to 30 degree bevel-up entry follows the vein path and reduces the chance of going through the back wall. A 45 degree or steeper angle increases the risk of transfixing the vein and striking underlying structures.

questions.q: When anchoring a vein before insertion, the phlebotomist should:
choices: Place the thumb above and below the site in a C shape
Pull the skin taut with the thumb 1 to 2 inches below the site
Press directly over the vein with two fingers
Ask the patient to hold the skin taut
questions.why: Anchoring below the site with the thumb keeps the vein from rolling without placing a finger in the needle path. Placing a finger above the site risks a needlestick to the phlebotomist during insertion.

questions.q: Blood is collected with a syringe and must be transferred to tubes. What is the correct technique?
choices: Remove tube stoppers and pour the blood in
Push the plunger firmly to speed filling
Recap the needle and pierce each stopper
Use a safety transfer device and let tube vacuum draw the blood in order of draw
questions.why: A transfer device lets each tube fill by its own vacuum, preserving the correct volume and preventing needlesticks. Forcing blood with the plunger causes hemolysis and can pop the stopper.

questions.q: When a butterfly set is used and a light blue citrate tube is the first tube needed, the phlebotomist should:
choices: Draw a discard tube first to fill the tubing dead space
Draw the citrate tube first and underfill it slightly
Prime the tubing with saline
Switch to a 21 gauge straight needle instead
questions.why: Air in the butterfly tubing would otherwise displace blood volume and short-draw the citrate tube, ruining the 9:1 ratio, so a discard tube is drawn first. Deliberately underfilling the citrate tube falsely prolongs PT and PTT.

questions.q: Which vein is the first choice for routine antecubital venipuncture?
choices: Basilic
Median cubital
Cephalic
Brachial
questions.why: The median cubital vein is large, well anchored, and sits away from the brachial artery and median nerve. The basilic vein is a last choice precisely because the nerve and artery lie close to it.

questions.q: A patient reports a sudden electric shock sensation shooting down the forearm as the needle is inserted. The phlebotomist should:
choices: Redirect the needle slightly deeper
Continue and complete the draw quickly
Remove the needle immediately and notify the supervisor
Loosen the tourniquet and continue
questions.why: Shooting pain, tingling, or numbness indicates nerve involvement and requires immediate needle removal and documentation. Continuing the draw risks permanent nerve injury.

questions.q: Bright red blood that pulses and rapidly fills the tube without vacuum assistance suggests:
choices: Arterial puncture
Hemolyzed venous blood
A collapsed vein
Tube vacuum loss
questions.why: Pulsatile bright red flow indicates the artery was entered; the needle should be removed and firm pressure held for at least 5 minutes, with the specimen labeled as possibly arterial. A collapsed vein produces the opposite picture, with flow stopping.

questions.q: A patient becomes pale, diaphoretic, and light-headed during a draw. The first action is to:
choices: Give the patient water to drink
Have the patient stand and walk it off
Apply an ammonia inhalant
Remove the needle, lower the patient's head, and protect the airway and from falling
questions.why: Syncope management starts with stopping the draw and preventing injury from a fall. Ammonia inhalants are not recommended because they can trigger bronchospasm in asthmatic patients.

questions.q: Small red pinpoint spots appearing on the arm after the tourniquet is applied are called:
choices: Ecchymosis
Petechiae
Hematoma
Purpura fulminans
questions.why: Petechiae are tiny capillary hemorrhages that may signal a platelet or capillary defect and warn of prolonged post-draw bleeding. A hematoma is a palpable collection of blood under the skin, not pinpoint spotting.

questions.q: A hematoma begins to form under the skin during a venipuncture. The phlebotomist should:
choices: Reposition the needle deeper and continue
Apply the tourniquet more tightly
Continue until the tube is full, then apply ice
Release the tourniquet, remove the needle, and apply firm pressure
questions.why: Blood leaking into tissue means the vein is compromised, so the draw is stopped and pressure applied to limit swelling and nerve compression. Tightening the tourniquet would increase leakage, not stop it.

questions.q: A patient is on warfarin and continues to ooze after the standard pressure period. The phlebotomist should:
choices: Hold direct pressure for at least 5 minutes and notify the nurse if bleeding continues
Apply a tight pressure bandage and leave immediately
Apply a warm compress
Have the patient bend the arm at the elbow
questions.why: Continued direct pressure for a full 5 minutes, with escalation if bleeding persists, is the standard. Bending the arm does not compress the site effectively and increases hematoma formation.

questions.q: A patient begins seizing during a venipuncture. The correct response is to:
choices: Place a padded tongue blade in the mouth
Restrain the arms until movement stops
Remove the needle and tourniquet, protect the patient from injury, and call for help
Continue the draw since the seizure is brief
questions.why: The needle must come out immediately and the patient is protected from striking objects while help is summoned; nothing is placed in the mouth and the patient is not restrained. Restraint can cause fractures and does not shorten the seizure.

questions.q: A patient reports a latex allergy. The phlebotomist should:
choices: Use a latex tourniquet but remove it quickly
Ask the patient to sign a waiver
Use latex gloves with powder to reduce contact
Use a nitrile or vinyl tourniquet and gloves and a non-latex bandage
questions.why: All latex-containing items in the encounter, including the tourniquet and adhesive bandage, must be replaced with latex-free alternatives. Shortening contact time does not prevent a reaction in a sensitized patient.

questions.q: For dermal puncture on a 3-month-old infant, the acceptable site is:
choices: The center (posterior curve) of the heel
The great toe pad
The medial or lateral plantar surface of the heel
The third finger of the left hand
questions.why: The medial and lateral plantar heel surfaces avoid the calcaneus, reducing the risk of osteomyelitis. Puncturing the posterior curve of the heel puts the lancet closest to the heel bone.

questions.q: When performing a finger stick on an adult, the preferred site is:
choices: The lateral side of the fleshy pad of the third or fourth finger
The tip of the index finger
The thumb pad
The fifth finger pad
questions.why: The middle or ring finger has adequate tissue and the lateral side avoids the denser central nerve endings and bone. The fifth finger has too little tissue between skin and bone, and the thumb and index finger are more callused and more heavily used.

questions.q: Why is the first drop of blood wiped away in a dermal puncture?
choices: It contains too many platelets
It is arterial rather than capillary
It is contaminated with tissue fluid and residual alcohol, which dilutes the sample
It clots faster than later drops
questions.why: The first drop carries interstitial fluid and alcohol residue that skew results and can cause hemolysis. Capillary blood is a mix of arterial, venous, and tissue fluid, so being arterial is not the reason.

questions.q: The correct order of draw for capillary collection is:
choices: Serum, then additive tubes, then EDTA
Additive tubes, then EDTA, then serum
EDTA, then serum, then other additives
EDTA, then other additive tubes, then serum tubes
questions.why: EDTA is filled first in capillary collection because platelet clumping and clotting begin quickly at the puncture site and would ruin the hematology sample. This is the reverse of the venipuncture order, where EDTA comes near the end.

questions.q: Vigorously squeezing or milking a finger during a dermal puncture most commonly causes:
choices: An elevated white blood cell count
Hemolysis and contamination with tissue fluid, falsely altering potassium and other results
Clotting of the serum tube
Falsely low bilirubin
questions.why: Milking ruptures red cells and forces interstitial fluid into the sample, which raises potassium and dilutes analytes. It does not selectively raise the white cell count.

questions.q: Which set of results is most affected by hemolysis?
choices: Potassium, LDH, AST, and magnesium
Sodium, chloride, and bicarbonate
Prothrombin time and fibrinogen
Total protein and albumin only
questions.why: These analytes are far more concentrated inside red cells, so cell rupture falsely elevates them. Sodium is actually higher outside the cell, so hemolysis has little upward effect on it.

questions.q: Which technique is a known cause of specimen hemolysis?
choices: Using a 21 gauge needle
Allowing the alcohol to air dry
Inverting tubes gently 8 times
Forcing blood through a needle from a syringe into a tube
questions.why: Shearing blood through a needle under plunger pressure ruptures red cells. Air drying alcohol actually prevents hemolysis, since wet alcohol lyses cells at the puncture site.

questions.q: A patient has an IV running in the left forearm and no acceptable veins in the right arm. The best action is to:
choices: Draw directly from the IV line without flushing
Draw from a site above the IV
Ask the nurse to stop the IV for 2 minutes, then draw below the IV site and note it on the requisition
Use the IV arm above the insertion point with a tourniquet
questions.why: Drawing distal to (below) a temporarily stopped IV minimizes dilution by the infusing fluid, and the circumstance must be documented. Drawing above the IV samples blood that has just mixed with the infusate and produces markedly falsified results.

questions.q: Blood drawn from a vascular access device (VAD) requires which step first?
choices: Flushing the line and discarding an appropriate volume before collecting the sample
Drawing the coagulation tube first with no discard
Removing the device and performing a standard venipuncture
Applying a tourniquet above the device
questions.why: Residual flush solution such as heparin or saline must be cleared with a discard volume or the results are contaminated and diluted. Drawing a coagulation tube without a discard is a classic cause of falsely prolonged PT and PTT.

questions.q: When must a specimen be labeled?
choices: At the nurses' station after all patients are drawn
At the patient's side immediately after collection, before leaving the room
Before the draw so the tubes are ready
In the laboratory at accessioning
questions.why: Bedside labeling before leaving the patient is the single strongest safeguard against misidentification. Prelabeling tubes is prohibited because tubes can be used on the wrong patient or left unused and misapplied.

questions.q: Which set of elements must appear on a specimen label?
choices: Patient name and room number only
Diagnosis, ordering provider, and test name
Patient name and the phlebotomist's initials only
Patient full name, unique identifier, date and time of collection, and collector's initials
questions.why: All four elements are required so the specimen can be traced and matched to the correct patient and time. Room number is not a unique identifier because patients are moved.

questions.q: A specimen arrives in the lab with a label bearing the correct name but no collection time. This specimen is most likely:
choices: Rejected as improperly labeled and a recollection requested
Accepted because the name matches
Corrected by the laboratory using the delivery time
Accepted for chemistry but not hematology
questions.why: Missing required label elements make the specimen unacceptable and it must be recollected. The laboratory cannot invent or infer a collection time, since timed tests depend on it.

questions.q: A royal blue tube is most often ordered for:
choices: Coagulation studies
Blood bank crossmatch
Trace element testing such as zinc, copper, or lead
Erythrocyte sedimentation rate
questions.why: Royal blue tubes are manufactured with very low background metal contamination for trace element and toxicology testing. Blood bank work uses pink or lavender EDTA tubes, not royal blue.

questions.q: Which tube is typically used for a type and screen or crossmatch?
choices: Green sodium heparin
Pink EDTA
Gray oxalate/fluoride
Light blue citrate
questions.why: Blood bank testing uses a pink EDTA tube (or lavender EDTA per facility policy) with special full-identification labeling requirements. Heparin interferes with antiglobulin testing and is unacceptable.

questions.q: An erythrocyte sedimentation rate (ESR) is most commonly performed on blood collected in:
choices: A gold SST
A gray tube
A green tube
A lavender EDTA tube or a black sodium citrate ESR tube
questions.why: EDTA or the dedicated black citrate ESR tube keeps cells intact and unclotted so the settling rate can be measured. Serum from an SST contains no cells to sediment.

questions.q: A lithium heparin green tube is unsuitable for which test?
choices: Ammonia
Lithium level
Electrolytes
Stat chemistry panel
questions.why: The lithium in the additive falsely elevates a lithium level, so sodium heparin is used instead. Lithium heparin is actually preferred for ammonia and routine electrolytes.

questions.q: How many times must a phlebotomist attempt a venipuncture before requesting assistance?
choices: Four attempts
Only one attempt is ever allowed
No more than two attempts, then ask another phlebotomist or the supervisor
As many as needed until successful
questions.why: The standard is a maximum of two attempts before handing off, to limit patient discomfort and tissue injury. There is no rule limiting a competent phlebotomist to a single attempt.

questions.q: Blind probing with the needle to locate a vein is discouraged primarily because it:
choices: Wastes tube vacuum
Increases the risk of nerve injury, arterial puncture, and hematoma
Causes the tourniquet to loosen
Always results in hemolysis
questions.why: Lateral probing drives the needle into structures the phlebotomist cannot see, most importantly nerves and arteries. Hemolysis is possible but is not the main hazard.

questions.q: Blood begins to flow and then abruptly stops, and the vein seems to disappear. The most likely cause is:
choices: Needle bevel resting against the vein wall
A collapsed vein from excessive vacuum on a small vessel
Loss of tube vacuum
The tourniquet being too loose
questions.why: A large tube's vacuum can pull a small or fragile vein shut; using a smaller tube or a syringe avoids it. A bevel against the wall usually produces sluggish or intermittent flow from the start rather than an abrupt stop after good flow.

questions.q: A tube is engaged on the needle and no blood enters at all, though the phlebotomist is confident of vein entry. The first troubleshooting step is to:
choices: Try a second tube, since the first may have lost its vacuum
Withdraw the needle completely and start over
Push the needle deeper
Remove the tourniquet
questions.why: A vacuum tube that was dropped or prepunctured will not fill, and changing tubes is the least invasive first check. Advancing the needle deeper risks going through the vein and causing a hematoma.

questions.q: A vein rolls away as the needle approaches. The best corrective action is to:
choices: Use a larger gauge needle
Insert at a 45 degree angle
Apply the tourniquet for 3 minutes first
Anchor the skin more firmly below the site before insertion
questions.why: Firm distal anchoring stabilizes the vessel so the bevel enters instead of pushing it aside. Leaving a tourniquet on for 3 minutes exceeds the 1 minute limit and causes hemoconcentration.

questions.q: The tourniquet should not remain in place longer than:
choices: 3 minutes
1 minute
5 minutes
30 seconds
questions.why: Beyond 1 minute, hemoconcentration falsely elevates analytes such as protein, calcium, and potassium. Longer limits like 3 or 5 minutes are not acceptable for routine collection.

questions.q: A tourniquet left on during the entire draw would most likely cause which preanalytical error?
choices: Hemoconcentration with falsely elevated total protein and cholesterol
Falsely low potassium
Clotted EDTA specimen
Falsely prolonged PT
questions.why: Venous stasis forces water out of the vessel and concentrates large molecules and cell-bound analytes. Potassium tends to rise rather than fall with prolonged stasis and fist pumping.

questions.q: Vigorous fist pumping before a draw should be avoided because it can falsely elevate:
choices: Glucose
Potassium
Sodium
Albumin
questions.why: Muscle contraction releases potassium from cells into the local circulation. Glucose is affected by fasting status and glycolysis, not by fist clenching.

questions.q: After the needle is withdrawn, the phlebotomist should:
choices: Apply the bandage immediately and let the patient hold pressure later
Have the patient bend the arm to compress the site
Apply direct pressure with clean gauze until bleeding stops, then bandage
Massage the site to disperse blood
questions.why: Direct pressure over the site until bleeding stops prevents hematoma, and only then is a bandage applied. Bending the arm is ineffective and is a frequent cause of bruising.

questions.q: An adhesive bandage should not be applied after a heel stick on a 6-month-old because:
choices: It interferes with the next collection
It slows clotting
Infants do not bruise
The adhesive can irritate or tear fragile skin and the bandage is a choking and aspiration hazard in children under 2
questions.why: Children under 2 years are at risk both from skin damage and from a loosened bandage entering the airway, so gauze and pressure are used instead. Bandages do not slow clotting.

questions.q: A contaminated needle must be:
choices: Disposed of in a sharps container at the point of use, without recapping
Recapped with one hand and then discarded
Cut from the hub before disposal
Placed in a red biohazard bag
questions.why: Point-of-use disposal of the activated safety device without recapping is the OSHA standard. Biohazard bags do not protect against punctures and are not sharps containers.

questions.q: A sharps container should be replaced when it is:
choices: Completely full to the rim
Full of only needles and no tube holders
Emptied weekly regardless of level
About two-thirds to three-quarters full
questions.why: Replacing at roughly three-quarters full prevents overfilling and protruding sharps. Filling to the rim forces staff to press items down and causes sticks.

questions.q: According to current OSHA guidance, the tube holder used with a needle should be:
choices: Reused after wiping with alcohol
Reused within the same patient encounter only
Autoclaved and reused
Discarded with the needle attached as a single unit
questions.why: Single-use disposal of the needle and holder together removes the risk of exposure during removal of the needle from the holder. Wiping with alcohol does not make a holder reusable.

questions.q: The alcohol pad should be allowed to air dry before venipuncture primarily because residual alcohol:
choices: Dulls the needle
Causes a stinging sensation and can hemolyze the specimen
Reacts with EDTA to form clots
Interferes with the tourniquet
questions.why: Wet alcohol lyses red cells entering the needle and burns on insertion. Alcohol has no chemical interaction with the tube additive through the needle in a way that produces clots.

questions.q: A blood alcohol level is ordered for legal purposes. The site should be cleaned with:
choices: 70 percent isopropyl alcohol
Benzalkonium chloride or another non-alcohol antiseptic
Tincture of iodine only
No antiseptic at all
questions.why: An alcohol-based prep could be challenged as a source of contamination in a legal specimen, so a non-alcohol antiseptic is used. Skipping antiseptic entirely violates infection control.

questions.q: Blood culture collection requires which skin preparation?
choices: Chlorhexidine or iodine scrub with the required contact time, then do not re-palpate the site
70 percent alcohol wiped once
Soap and water only
Alcohol followed by immediate palpation to confirm the vein
questions.why: An extended antiseptic contact time is required to reduce skin flora, and touching the site afterward recontaminates it. Re-palpating after prep is a leading cause of false-positive cultures.

questions.q: When collecting two blood culture bottles, the recommended fill order and volume handling is:
choices: Fill the anaerobic bottle first from a syringe
Overfill both bottles to improve yield
Fill only one bottle and split it later
Fill the aerobic bottle first when using a butterfly and winged set, because air in the tubing would enter the anaerobic bottle
questions.why: Tubing air would displace the anaerobic environment, so the aerobic bottle takes it first with a winged set. Overfilling dilutes the medium ratio and can cause false results.

questions.q: A fasting glucose specimen is collected in a gray tube. If it were collected in an SST and left at room temperature for several hours, the glucose would:
choices: Rise steadily
Remain unchanged
Fall by roughly 5 to 7 percent per hour due to glycolysis
Become falsely elevated by hemolysis
questions.why: Cells continue consuming glucose in the tube unless an antiglycolytic agent such as sodium fluoride is present or the serum is separated promptly. Hemolysis does not raise glucose.

questions.q: A patient states they had coffee with cream 2 hours ago before a fasting lipid panel. The phlebotomist should:
choices: Draw anyway and say nothing
Cancel the order
Notify the appropriate person and document the non-fasting status per policy
Have the patient wait 30 minutes and then draw
questions.why: Fasting status is a preanalytical variable that must be communicated and documented rather than concealed. Canceling the order is outside the phlebotomist's scope; the provider decides.

questions.q: Which of the following is a preanalytical error?
choices: Mislabeling a tube at the nurses' station
An instrument calibration drift
A transcription error in the final report
An incorrect reference range in the LIS
questions.why: Preanalytical errors occur before testing, and identification and collection mistakes are the largest category. Calibration drift is analytical and report transcription is postanalytical.

questions.q: Before drawing an inpatient, the phlebotomist should identify the patient by:
choices: Reading the name on the door
Asking the patient to state full name and date of birth and comparing to the armband and requisition
Asking the roommate to confirm
Matching the room and bed number to the requisition
questions.why: Active identification with two identifiers verified against the armband and requisition is required. Door signs, roommates, and room numbers are not reliable identifiers.

questions.q: A patient scheduled for a mastectomy-side draw has had a left mastectomy 3 weeks ago. The phlebotomist should:
choices: Draw from the left arm using a smaller gauge needle
Draw from the left hand instead
Use the right arm and, if unavailable, obtain provider approval before using the affected side
Use the left arm without a tourniquet
questions.why: Lymphedema risk and altered analyte values make the affected side off limits without provider authorization. Changing the gauge or omitting the tourniquet does not remove the lymphatic risk.

questions.q: Dorsal hand veins are an acceptable alternative site, but the phlebotomist should:
choices: Use an 18 gauge straight needle
Insert at a 45 degree angle
Use a winged set with a smaller gauge and a shallow angle because hand veins are small and superficial
Omit the tourniquet entirely
questions.why: A 23 gauge butterfly at a shallow angle matches the small, superficial vessels and reduces the chance of going through them. A large-bore needle at a steep angle almost guarantees a blown vein.

questions.q: Which site should be avoided for routine venipuncture?
choices: The median cubital vein of the right arm
The cephalic vein of the forearm
An area of extensive scarring or burns
A dorsal hand vein
questions.why: Scarred and burned tissue has impaired circulation and is painful and difficult to enter, giving unreliable results. Cephalic and dorsal hand veins are acceptable alternatives when the median cubital is unavailable.

questions.q: A phlebotomist is asked to draw from a patient's arm with a functioning arteriovenous fistula. The correct action is to:
choices: Avoid that arm entirely and use the other arm
Draw distal to the fistula with a tourniquet
Draw directly from the fistula
Use the fistula arm without a tourniquet
questions.why: A fistula is the patient's dialysis lifeline and must not be compromised or punctured by phlebotomy. Only specially trained dialysis staff access a fistula.

questions.q: Green-top heparin tubes require how many inversions and why?
choices: 0 inversions because heparin is a coating
3 to 4 inversions to prevent hemolysis
8 to 10 inversions to mix the heparin and prevent clotting
30 inversions to activate antithrombin
questions.why: Heparin tubes need 8 to 10 gentle inversions to distribute the additive and prevent microclots in the plasma. Heparin is a real additive, not an inert coating, so inversions are required.

questions.q: Potassium oxalate acts as an anticoagulant by:
choices: Inhibiting thrombin through antithrombin III
Precipitating calcium into an insoluble salt
Activating fibrinolysis
Coating the tube with silicone
questions.why: Oxalate removes calcium from the clotting cascade by precipitation, which is why it distorts cell morphology and is paired with fluoride for glucose tubes. Thrombin inhibition through antithrombin III describes heparin.

questions.q: A gold SST tube contains:
choices: Sodium citrate and a gel plug
EDTA and a clot activator
A clot activator and a thixotropic separator gel
Lithium heparin and gel
questions.why: Silica clot activator plus a separator gel yields serum ready for chemistry after centrifugation. A plasma separator tube (PST, light green) is the one containing lithium heparin and gel.

questions.q: A specimen must be protected from light. Which analyte most commonly requires this?
choices: Potassium
Bilirubin
Sodium
Chloride
questions.why: Bilirubin degrades on light exposure, giving falsely low results, so the tube is wrapped in foil or an amber container. Electrolytes are not light sensitive.

questions.q: A cold agglutinin specimen requires which handling?
choices: Chilled in ice slurry
Frozen immediately
Kept at 37 degrees C until the serum is separated
Protected from light
questions.why: Cooling would let the agglutinins bind red cells and falsely lower the serum titer, so the specimen is kept warm. Chilling is the requirement for ammonia and lactic acid, not cold agglutinins.

questions.q: An ammonia specimen should be:
choices: Kept at 37 degrees C
Held at room temperature for 2 hours
Placed on ice and delivered promptly
Protected from light only
questions.why: Chilling slows the metabolic production of ammonia in the tube, preserving the true level. Warming at 37 degrees is the opposite of what this analyte needs.

questions.q: After centrifugation, serum or plasma should generally be separated from cells within:
choices: 30 minutes of collection
2 hours of collection
8 hours of collection
24 hours of collection
questions.why: Two hours is the standard limit before cellular metabolism and analyte shift compromise results, most notably potassium and glucose. Eight or 24 hours far exceeds acceptable stability for routine chemistry.

questions.q: A tube of blood is refrigerated whole and uncentrifuged overnight before a potassium is run. The result will likely be:
