choices: Falsely elevated because cold inhibits the cellular pump and potassium leaks out
Falsely low
Accurate
Unreportable due to clotting
questions.why: Refrigeration inactivates the sodium-potassium ATPase, letting potassium escape into the serum. The error is an artifactual increase, not a decrease.

questions.q: Which is a valid specimen rejection criterion?
choices: The tube is filled to the fill line
The tube was inverted 8 times
A grossly hemolyzed specimen submitted for potassium
The specimen arrived within 1 hour
questions.why: Gross hemolysis makes potassium and several enzymes unreportable, so the specimen is rejected and recollected. Proper filling, mixing, and prompt delivery are all signs of an acceptable specimen.

questions.q: A phlebotomist notices a lavender tube with small clots after transport. The correct action is to:
choices: Remove the clots with an applicator stick and submit
Submit it and note the clots on the requisition
Centrifuge it and run the plasma
Reject the specimen and recollect, since clots invalidate cell counts
questions.why: Clotting means cells and platelets have been consumed, so the CBC is unreliable and only a new draw fixes it. Removing clots does not restore the cells already trapped in them.

questions.q: Which documentation is required after every draw?
choices: The manufacturer lot number of the gloves
Date, time, collector identification, and any unusual circumstance such as a difficult draw or IV arm
The patient's diagnosis
The centrifuge speed used
questions.why: Traceable collection details and notable circumstances let the lab and provider interpret results correctly. Diagnosis and instrument parameters are not the phlebotomist's documentation responsibility.

questions.q: A trace element zinc level is drawn along with a CBC and a chemistry panel. The royal blue trace tube should be:
choices: Drawn first, before the blood culture
Drawn last after the gray tube
Drawn in the position matching its additive, and generally before other additive tubes to avoid contamination
Drawn only by syringe
questions.why: Trace element tubes are placed to minimize carryover of metal-containing additives from other tubes, following the facility's CLSI-based protocol for its additive. Blood cultures still precede all tubes, so it is never truly first.

questions.q: A phlebotomist inserts the needle and gets a small flash of blood, then flow stops. The needle is likely:
choices: Completely through the far wall of the vein
Bevel resting against the upper vein wall, which can be corrected by slightly rotating or withdrawing the needle a fraction
In an artery
In a collapsed vein
questions.why: A brief flash with cessation of flow typically means the bevel is occluded against the vessel wall, and a small rotation or pullback restores flow. Passing through the far wall usually gives no flow at all and a developing hematoma.

questions.q: The primary reason a discard tube is required before a coagulation draw through a winged set is:
choices: To warm the tubing
To clear tissue thromboplastin from the first blood
To displace the air in the tubing so the citrate tube fills to its correct volume
To check the needle for a burr
questions.why: The tubing dead space would otherwise steal volume from the citrate tube and break the 9:1 ratio. With modern practice, a plain discard tube is used for volume, not to clear thromboplastin, which is no longer the accepted rationale for routine PT/PTT.

questions.q: When a syringe draw is performed, the order of draw:
choices: Does not apply, because there is no additive contact
Reverses completely
Still applies as tubes are filled through the transfer device
Applies only if a butterfly is used
questions.why: Carryover between tubes still occurs during transfer, so the standard order is maintained. The order is never reversed for a syringe; only capillary collection has a different order.

questions.q: A phlebotomist should position an outpatient for venipuncture:
choices: Standing at a counter
Seated in a chair with an armrest, or reclining if there is a history of fainting
Seated on a stool with no back
Lying on the floor
questions.why: An armrest chair supports the arm and prevents falls, and a reclining position is used when syncope is a known risk. A backless stool or standing position offers no fall protection.

questions.q: Gloves should be changed:
choices: Only when visibly soiled
Once per shift
Between every patient
Only after contact with blood
questions.why: Gloves are changed between every patient regardless of visible soiling to prevent cross-contamination. Waiting for visible soil or blood contact is well past the point of transmission risk.

questions.q: A slightly short draw in which tube is most likely to still produce acceptable results?
choices: Light blue sodium citrate
Gray potassium oxalate/sodium fluoride
Lavender EDTA
Gold SST with clot activator and gel
questions.why: Serum tubes have no liquid additive ratio to preserve, so a modestly underfilled SST usually still yields valid results if enough serum is obtained. Citrate is the least forgiving because of the strict 9:1 ratio requirement.

questions.q: A phlebotomist is preparing a patient's antecubital site for a blood culture using chlorhexidine gluconate. How long should the scrub be performed before the site is allowed to dry?
choices: 10 seconds
15 seconds
30 seconds
2 minutes
questions.why: Chlorhexidine gluconate requires a 30-second friction scrub followed by complete air drying to kill skin flora. A 15-second scrub is the common distractor but does not provide adequate contact time, and undried antiseptic can inhibit organism growth.

questions.q: When blood cultures are collected with a syringe on an adult, which bottle is inoculated first and why?
choices: Aerobic, because air in the syringe would be pushed into the anaerobic bottle
Anaerobic, because anaerobes die fastest
Either bottle, because volume is what matters
Aerobic, because it holds more media
questions.why: With a syringe draw, the aerobic bottle is filled first so residual air in the syringe hub does not enter the anaerobic bottle and kill the anaerobes. With a butterfly and holder the order reverses, which is why simply answering anaerobic first is wrong.

questions.q: An adult blood culture set is being collected. What volume of blood should be placed in each bottle?
choices: 1 to 3 mL
3 to 5 mL
5 to 7 mL
8 to 10 mL
questions.why: Adult bottles require 8 to 10 mL each because bacteremia is often low level and sensitivity rises with volume. The 1 to 3 mL range applies to pediatric bottles, not adults.

questions.q: A provider orders two sets of blood cultures. Which collection approach is correct?
choices: Both sets from the same vein back to back
Two sets drawn from two separate venipuncture sites
One set from a vein and one from a capillary stick
Both sets from the existing peripheral IV
questions.why: Two sets from two different sites let the lab distinguish true bacteremia from skin contamination, since the same organism in both sites suggests true infection. Drawing both from one site defeats that comparison.

questions.q: A blood culture grows coagulase-negative Staphylococcus in one bottle of one set only, while the second site is negative. This pattern most likely indicates which of the following?
choices: Skin flora contamination during collection
True gram-negative sepsis
Endocarditis requiring immediate surgery
A false-negative culture
questions.why: A common skin organism growing in only one bottle of one set is the classic picture of contamination from inadequate antisepsis. True bacteremia typically produces growth in both sets drawn from separate sites.

questions.q: When is the optimal time to collect blood cultures relative to a patient's fever and antibiotic schedule?
choices: At the peak of the fever, after the antibiotic dose
Twenty-four hours after antibiotics are started
As the fever is rising and before the next antibiotic dose
Only when the patient is afebrile
questions.why: Organism concentration is highest as the temperature spikes, and drawing before the antibiotic dose (at the trough) avoids drug suppression of growth. Collecting after the dose lowers recovery of the organism.

questions.q: A patient needs blood cultures, a light blue citrate tube, a green heparin tube, and a lavender EDTA tube. Which is collected first?
choices: Light blue citrate
Blood culture bottles
Green heparin
Lavender EDTA
questions.why: Sterile blood culture bottles always precede all other tubes in the CLSI order of draw to protect sterility. Light blue is first among the additive tubes but still follows the cultures.

questions.q: A phlebotomist is collecting a newborn screening card by heelstick. Which technique is correct?
choices: Layer several small drops into each circle until filled
Press the card directly against the heel and smear
Fill the circles from both sides of the paper
Apply one large free-flowing drop to fill each circle completely
questions.why: Each circle must be filled with a single large drop allowed to soak through and saturate the paper evenly. Layering multiple drops creates uneven saturation and is a top cause of rejected newborn screening cards.

questions.q: After collection, how should a newborn screening card be handled before transport?
choices: Sealed in a plastic bag immediately
Placed under a warming lamp to speed drying
Air dried flat at room temperature away from heat and sunlight
Refrigerated while still wet
questions.why: The card must dry flat in open air at room temperature for at least three hours; heat, sunlight, and sealing in plastic denature the analytes. A warming lamp accelerates drying but destroys specimen integrity.

questions.q: A bilirubin specimen is collected on a jaundiced neonate. What special handling is required?
choices: Protect the specimen from light using an amber tube or foil wrap
Keep the specimen at 37 degrees C
Place the specimen in an ice slurry
Agitate the specimen continuously
questions.why: Bilirubin is photosensitive and can degrade significantly within an hour of light exposure, falsely lowering results. Chilling is required for ammonia and lactic acid, not bilirubin.

questions.q: A cold agglutinin specimen is ordered. Which handling is correct?
choices: Chill in ice water immediately after collection
Collect in EDTA and refrigerate
Warm the tube to 37 degrees C and keep it warm until the serum is separated
Freeze the specimen within 30 minutes
questions.why: Cold agglutinins attach to red cells below body temperature, so the specimen must be prewarmed and maintained at 37 degrees C until serum separation. Refrigerating it removes the antibody from the serum and falsely lowers the titer.

questions.q: Which of the following specimens requires transport in an ice slurry?
choices: Cold agglutinins
Ammonia and lactic acid
Bilirubin
Cryoglobulins
questions.why: Ammonia and lactic acid rise rapidly through in vitro cell metabolism, so chilling slows that change. Cold agglutinins and cryoglobulins require 37 degrees C transport, the opposite condition.

questions.q: A three-hour glucose tolerance test is ordered. Which patient preparation is correct?
choices: The patient may eat a light breakfast before the fasting draw
The patient should chew gum to stay hydrated
The patient should smoke to reduce anxiety
The patient fasts 8 to 12 hours, and may drink only water before the fasting specimen
questions.why: A valid GTT begins with a true 8 to 12 hour fast in which only water is permitted. Gum, food, and smoking all stimulate digestion or glucose changes and invalidate the baseline.

questions.q: During a glucose tolerance test, the timing of each timed specimen is counted from which point?
choices: The time the patient finishes drinking the glucose beverage
The time the fasting specimen was drawn
The time the patient arrived at the lab
The time the provider ordered the test
questions.why: All timed intervals start the moment the patient finishes the glucose load, since that is when absorption begins. Timing from the fasting draw shifts every subsequent collection and makes the curve uninterpretable.

questions.q: Thirty minutes into a glucose tolerance test, a patient vomits the glucose beverage. What should the phlebotomist do?
choices: Continue the test and note the vomiting later
Give a second glucose drink and restart the clock
Notify the provider, who decides whether to stop or reschedule the test
Collect all remaining specimens early
questions.why: Vomiting means the glucose load was not absorbed, so the provider must decide whether to abort or reschedule. A phlebotomist may not independently redose a patient with glucose.

questions.q: A trough level for vancomycin should be collected at which time?
choices: Immediately before the next scheduled dose
Thirty minutes after the infusion ends
Halfway between two doses
Any time during the infusion
questions.why: The trough is the lowest concentration and is drawn immediately before the next dose, usually within 30 minutes of it. A specimen drawn 30 minutes after the infusion reflects the peak, not the trough.

questions.q: A gentamicin peak level is ordered. When is it typically collected?
choices: Immediately before the dose
Twelve hours after the dose
Twenty-four hours after the dose
About 30 minutes after the IV infusion is complete
questions.why: Peak levels for aminoglycosides are drawn about 30 minutes after the end of an IV infusion, when distribution is complete. Drawing before the dose yields the trough and would be reported incorrectly if labeled a peak.

questions.q: A digoxin level is ordered on a patient who received an oral dose one hour ago. What is the most appropriate action?
choices: Draw immediately since digoxin is stable
Draw and mark the specimen as a peak
Notify the nurse that digoxin levels require at least 8 hours after the dose for equilibration
Refuse the order outright
questions.why: Digoxin distributes slowly into tissue, so a level drawn before roughly 8 hours post-dose is falsely elevated. Drawing it early and labeling it a peak would mislead the provider into reducing a correct dose.

questions.q: Which site preparation is required for a legal blood alcohol collection?
choices: 70 percent isopropyl alcohol
A non-alcohol antiseptic such as povidone-iodine or benzalkonium chloride
Chlorhexidine gluconate with alcohol base
No antiseptic at all
questions.why: An alcohol-based prep can contaminate the specimen and is indefensible in court, so a non-alcohol antiseptic is used. Isopropyl alcohol is the standard venipuncture prep but is specifically prohibited here.

questions.q: Which tube is generally used for a blood alcohol specimen, and why?
choices: Lavender EDTA, to prevent clotting
Light blue citrate, to preserve plasma
Red serum tube, because no additive interferes
Gray sodium fluoride and potassium oxalate, because fluoride inhibits glycolysis and microbial alcohol production
questions.why: Sodium fluoride in the gray tube blocks glycolysis and stops microbes from fermenting glucose into ethanol, which would falsely raise the result. A red serum tube offers no such preservative protection.

questions.q: A blood alcohol specimen is collected for law enforcement. What documentation is required?
choices: A standard requisition only
A chain of custody form documenting every person who handles the specimen
A verbal report to the officer
A copy of the patient's chart
questions.why: Forensic specimens require an unbroken, signed chain of custody from collection through analysis to be admissible. A routine requisition does not document transfer of possession.

questions.q: During a urine drug screen collection, the specimen temperature must be checked within what time frame?
choices: Within 4 minutes of voiding
Within 15 minutes
Within 30 minutes
Within 1 hour
questions.why: The temperature strip must be read within 4 minutes, and an acceptable range is 32.5 to 37.7 degrees C, to detect a substituted specimen. Waiting 15 or 30 minutes lets the sample cool and destroys the check.

questions.q: In a federally regulated split specimen drug collection, how is the urine handled?
choices: The entire volume is sent as one sample
Two separate voids are collected an hour apart
The single void is divided into an A bottle for testing and a B bottle held for possible retest
The donor keeps half the sample
questions.why: One void is split into bottles A and B, with B sealed and stored so the donor may request confirmatory retesting. Collecting two separate voids would not be a split of the same specimen and is not acceptable.

questions.q: Which action best protects the integrity of a forensic specimen collection?
choices: Leaving the specimen at the nurses station for pickup
Sealing the specimen in tamper-evident packaging and documenting each transfer with signatures and times
Labeling the specimen after transport
Storing it unlabeled in a locked drawer
questions.why: Tamper-evident sealing plus signed, timed transfers proves the specimen was never altered or exchanged. Any unattended or unlabeled interval breaks the chain and makes the result inadmissible.

questions.q: A phlebotomist is collecting specimens for paternity testing. Which requirement applies?
choices: Positive identification of every participant with photo ID, chain of custody, and specimens from mother, child, and alleged father
Only the child needs to be identified
Specimens may be collected at home and mailed in
Verbal identification by a relative is sufficient
questions.why: Parentage testing is a legal collection requiring photo identification of each party and full chain of custody on all three specimens. Relying on a relative to vouch for identity would invalidate the result in court.

questions.q: Before drawing a type and crossmatch, which identification step is required?
choices: Confirm the room number with the unit clerk
Ask the patient to confirm the ordering provider
Check the chart for a prior blood type
Compare the patient's stated name and date of birth to the ID band and requisition, and apply the blood bank identification band
questions.why: Active identification against the ID band plus a blood bank band that links the patient to the specimen prevents fatal ABO mismatches. Room number is never an acceptable identifier because patients are moved.

questions.q: A blood bank specimen label must include which item not required on a routine chemistry label?
choices: Test name
Patient name
Date of collection
The phlebotomist's initials and the blood bank band number tying the specimen to the patient
questions.why: The blood bank band number and collector identification create a traceable link from the crossmatch specimen to the patient at the bedside. Name and date appear on routine labels too and do not provide that link.

questions.q: A patient scheduled for elective hip surgery donates units of her own blood in advance. This is called what?
choices: Directed donation
Therapeutic phlebotomy
Autologous donation
Apheresis
questions.why: Autologous donation means the patient donates blood for her own later transfusion, eliminating compatibility and disease transmission risk. A directed donation comes from a specific person chosen by the patient, not from the patient herself.

questions.q: A patient with hereditary hemochromatosis has a standing order for unit removal. This procedure is best described as which of the following?
choices: Therapeutic phlebotomy to reduce iron overload
Autologous donation for future use
Plasmapheresis
A diagnostic venipuncture
questions.why: Therapeutic phlebotomy removes a unit of blood as treatment, lowering iron stores in hemochromatosis or red cell mass in polycythemia vera. The blood is removed for treatment, not banked for the patient's own transfusion as in autologous donation.

questions.q: What is the approximate volume of a standard whole blood donor unit?
choices: 250 mL
350 mL
450 to 500 mL
750 mL
questions.why: A standard whole blood unit is about 450 to 500 mL, roughly one pint, collected into anticoagulant. Drawing 750 mL would exceed the safe limit for a single donation.

questions.q: A 19-year-old weighing 108 pounds with a hemoglobin of 13.5 g/dL wishes to donate whole blood. What is the correct action?
choices: Accept the donor, since the hemoglobin is adequate
Defer the donor, because the minimum weight for whole blood donation is 110 pounds
Defer the donor because of age
Accept but collect only half a unit
questions.why: Allogeneic whole blood donors must weigh at least 110 pounds so that the approximately 500 mL draw is a safe fraction of blood volume. The hemoglobin and age both meet criteria, which makes weight the only disqualifier.

questions.q: Before radial artery puncture, the modified Allen test is performed to determine what?
choices: That collateral circulation from the ulnar artery is adequate
That the patient is not anemic
That the radial pulse is strong
That the patient is not on anticoagulants
questions.why: The modified Allen test confirms the ulnar artery can perfuse the hand if the radial artery becomes occluded after puncture. A strong radial pulse says nothing about collateral ulnar flow, which is the actual safety concern.

questions.q: A modified Allen test is performed and the hand does not flush within 15 seconds after the ulnar artery is released. What does this mean?
choices: The test is positive and the site may be used
The patient is dehydrated
The phlebotomist should puncture the brachial artery instead without further evaluation
The test is negative and that radial artery must not be used
questions.why: Failure to flush indicates inadequate ulnar collateral circulation, so puncturing that radial artery risks ischemia of the hand. Selecting another site is a provider decision, not an automatic move to the brachial artery by the phlebotomist.

questions.q: Which syringe and handling combination is correct for an arterial blood gas specimen?
choices: A plain syringe transported at room temperature
A heparinized syringe with air bubbles expelled, capped and transported per protocol, often in ice slurry if delayed
An EDTA syringe kept at 37 degrees C
A citrate syringe protected from light
questions.why: ABGs require heparin anticoagulation, immediate removal of air bubbles because room air alters pO2 and pCO2, and chilling when analysis is delayed beyond 30 minutes. EDTA is never used because it alters pH.

questions.q: Who may perform an arterial puncture for blood gases?
choices: Any phlebotomist after basic venipuncture training
Only personnel with documented specialized arterial puncture training, such as respiratory therapists, nurses, or specially trained phlebotomists
A patient care technician under general supervision
Any staff member certified in CPR
questions.why: Arterial puncture carries risk of hemorrhage, nerve injury, and thrombosis, so it requires documented advanced training and institutional authorization. Routine venipuncture certification alone does not qualify a phlebotomist.

questions.q: A capillary blood gas is ordered on an infant. Which step is essential to a valid result?
choices: Squeezing the heel firmly to obtain flow quickly
Using the central plantar surface of the heel
Air drying the sample before capping
Prewarming the site and collecting free-flowing blood without air bubbles in the capillary tube
questions.why: Prewarming arterializes capillary blood and free flow without bubbles preserves gas values; squeezing introduces tissue fluid and falsely alters results. The central plantar surface risks bone injury and is never used for heelsticks.

questions.q: A glucose meter quality control result falls outside the acceptable range. What should the phlebotomist do?
choices: Run the patient sample anyway and flag the result
Repeat the control once and report the patient result regardless
Adjust the meter reading manually
Remove the meter from use, document the failure, and troubleshoot or use a backup device before testing patients
questions.why: An out of range control means patient results from that device cannot be trusted, so it must be taken out of service until resolved. Reporting a flagged patient result on a failed device still releases unreliable data.

questions.q: A point-of-care glucose reads critically high on a symptomatic patient. What is the appropriate next step?
choices: Notify the provider and collect a venous specimen for laboratory confirmation
Repeat the POC test three more times and average the values
Document the result and take no further action
Discard the result as an obvious error
questions.why: Critical POC values are screening results and must be confirmed by a laboratory method while the provider is notified promptly. Averaging repeated POC readings does not improve accuracy and delays treatment.

questions.q: A patient must collect a 24-hour urine specimen. Which instruction is correct?
choices: Save every void including the first morning specimen that starts the collection
Refrigerate only the final sample
Discard the first void, then collect all urine for 24 hours including the void at the end of the period, keeping the container cool
Collect only daytime voids
questions.why: The timed period starts with an empty bladder, so the first void is discarded and the final void at the 24-hour mark is included, with refrigeration or a preservative maintained throughout. Saving that first void adds urine made before the timed period and falsely raises analyte totals.

questions.q: A phlebotomist is instructing a female patient on a clean-catch midstream urine collection. Which instruction is correct?
choices: Collect the very first portion of the stream
Cleanse from front to back, begin voiding into the toilet, then collect the midstream portion in the sterile cup
Cleanse after voiding to avoid contaminating the wipe
Use tap water only, since antiseptic wipes interfere with culture
questions.why: Front to back cleansing plus discarding the initial stream washes away urethral and perineal flora so the midstream portion reflects bladder urine. Collecting the first portion carries the highest contamination and commonly causes mixed-flora culture rejection.

questions.q: A phlebotomist finishes a draw at the bedside. When should the tubes be labeled?
choices: After returning to the laboratory so the labels stay clean
Before the draw, so the tubes are ready to go
At the bedside, immediately after the draw and before leaving the patient
At the time the specimen is logged into the LIS
questions.why: Labeling occurs at the point of collection in the presence of the patient, which is the only way to guarantee the tube matches the patient. Labeling before the draw is wrong because an unused or aborted tube could then be filled with another patient's blood.

questions.q: A tube arrives in the laboratory with a legible label but the patient name does not match the name on the requisition. What is the correct action?
choices: Reject the specimen, notify the ordering unit, and document the discrepancy
Correct the tube label to match the requisition and process it
Process the specimen and add a comment to the report
Ask the nurse to verbally confirm which name is right, then relabel
questions.why: A mislabeled specimen cannot be corrected by anyone other than the original collector at the bedside, so it is rejected, documented, and the unit is notified for recollection. Relabeling from the requisition is prohibited because it only guesses at identity and can transfer a fatal error into the result.

questions.q: A red-top serum tube is drawn at 0800. How long should it sit before centrifugation?
choices: Spin immediately to save turnaround time
5 to 10 minutes
15 minutes maximum
30 to 60 minutes at room temperature to allow complete clotting
questions.why: Serum tubes need 30 to 60 minutes at room temperature for the clot to fully form before spinning. Spinning early leaves fibrin that continues to clot in the serum, producing latent fibrin strands that clog analyzer probes.

questions.q: Which statement correctly distinguishes serum from plasma?
choices: Serum contains fibrinogen; plasma does not
Serum is from a clotted, non-anticoagulated tube and lacks fibrinogen; plasma is from an anticoagulated tube and contains fibrinogen
Plasma comes from a red-top tube and serum from a lavender-top tube
Serum and plasma are chemically identical, only the tube color differs
questions.why: Clotting consumes fibrinogen, so serum has none, while an anticoagulated tube prevents clotting and leaves fibrinogen in the plasma. The first choice reverses the relationship, which is a classic trap.

questions.q: A phlebotomist has only one tube to centrifuge. What must be done before starting the spin?
choices: Place a balance tube of equal size filled with water to the same level opposite it
Spin the single tube at half speed
Place the tube in the center well of the rotor
Run the centrifuge with the lid open to monitor it
questions.why: The rotor must be balanced by weight and position, so a water-filled tube of the same size and fill level goes directly opposite. Reducing the speed does not correct an unbalanced load and can still damage the rotor and break tubes.

questions.q: A typical laboratory centrifuge setting for separating a serum gel tube is about:
choices: 1000 rpm for 2 minutes
1500 rpm for 20 minutes
3000 rpm for 10 minutes, following the manufacturer's instructions
5000 rpm for 15 minutes
questions.why: About 3000 rpm for 10 minutes is the common specification, but the tube and centrifuge manufacturer's directions always govern. Lower speed or shorter time gives incomplete separation and a poor gel barrier.

questions.q: A gel separator tube was spun once, and the barrier looks incomplete. The technician wants to spin it again. What is correct?
choices: Re-spin at a higher speed to force the gel down
Do not re-spin a gel tube; recollect the specimen if separation is inadequate
Re-spin for double the original time
Invert the tube and re-spin it upside down
questions.why: Re-spinning a gel tube can force analytes, especially potassium, out of cells trapped above or within the gel and falsely alter results. Higher speed does not fix the barrier and simply compounds the contamination.

questions.q: The centrifuge timer ends but the rotor is still coasting. What should the phlebotomist do?
choices: Open the lid and brake the rotor by hand to save time
Open the lid as soon as the timer stops
Open the lid and remove only the outer tubes
Wait until the rotor comes to a complete stop on its own before opening the lid
questions.why: Opening the lid or stopping the rotor by hand creates aerosols and can cause injury and tube breakage. Waiting for a full stop is the only safe practice, regardless of turnaround pressure.

questions.q: A serum specimen is drawn at 0900 and remains unspun on the counter. By what time must the serum be separated from the cells?
choices: 1100, which is 2 hours from the time of collection
There is no limit as long as the tube is capped
questions.why: The standard is separation of serum or plasma from cells within 2 hours of collection. Leaving cells in contact longer allows glycolysis and cellular leakage that invalidate several chemistry results.

questions.q: A potassium and glucose specimen sat with cells in contact for 4 hours. What results are expected?
choices: Both potassium and glucose falsely elevated
Potassium falsely elevated and glucose falsely decreased by roughly 10 mg/dL per hour
Potassium falsely decreased and glucose falsely increased
Neither analyte is affected if the tube stayed capped
questions.why: Red cells leak potassium into the serum while continuing glycolysis, consuming glucose at roughly 10 mg/dL per hour. Assuming a capped tube protects the sample is wrong because the change is cellular metabolism, not evaporation.

questions.q: Which group of tests requires the specimen to be chilled in an ice slurry during transport?
choices: Potassium, calcium, and magnesium
Bilirubin, folate, and vitamin B12
Ammonia, lactic acid, arterial blood gas, PTH, and gastrin
Cold agglutinins and cryoglobulins
questions.why: Ammonia, lactic acid, ABG, PTH, and gastrin are all unstable at room temperature and are chilled to slow metabolism and degradation. Cold agglutinins and cryoglobulins are the opposite case and must be kept at body temperature.

questions.q: A phlebotomist places a lavender-top chemistry specimen for potassium on ice. Why is this incorrect?
choices: Chilling causes red cells to release potassium, falsely elevating the result
Chilling causes potassium to bind to the tube wall, falsely lowering the result
Chilling has no measurable effect on potassium
Chilling causes the EDTA to precipitate
questions.why: Cold inhibits the cell membrane sodium-potassium pump, so potassium leaks out of the cells and the measured value rises falsely. It is not a falsely low value, which is the distractor most students pick by analogy to glucose.

questions.q: Which specimens must be protected from light during transport and storage?
choices: Ammonia and lactic acid
Cold agglutinins and cryoglobulins
PT and PTT specimens
Bilirubin, vitamin B12, folate, and carotene
questions.why: Bilirubin, vitamin B12, folate, and carotene photodegrade, so they are wrapped in foil or placed in an amber container. Ammonia and lactic acid need chilling rather than light protection.

questions.q: A cryoglobulin specimen is collected. How must it be handled before processing?
choices: Placed in an ice slurry immediately
Refrigerated at 2 to 8 C
Kept at 37 C body temperature until the serum is separated
Frozen at -20 C within 30 minutes
questions.why: Cryoglobulins and cold agglutinins precipitate or attach to cells when cooled, so the specimen stays at 37 C using a warming block or pre-warmed tube until separation. Icing would remove the very protein the test is designed to detect.

questions.q: A phlebotomist pours serum from a spun gel tube into a labeled transfer tube for a send-out test. What must the aliquot label contain?
choices: Only the accession number, since the parent tube has the rest
The same patient identifiers and accession information as the original tube
The technician's initials only
A new accession number generated at the time of pouring
questions.why: Every aliquot carries the full identification of the parent specimen so identity is never lost at any step. An accession number alone is insufficient if the tube leaves the facility or the label is questioned.

questions.q: Two tubes of serum from the same patient are short-draw. May they be combined into one aliquot tube to make enough volume?
choices: No. Pooling specimens is not permitted, even from the same patient, because collection times and additives may differ
Yes, as long as both tubes are the same color
Yes, if the technician documents the pooling
Yes, if both tubes were drawn within 2 hours of each other
questions.why: Pooling destroys the one-to-one link between a result and a single documented collection event and can mix different draw times or additives. Same tube color does not make the two collections interchangeable.

questions.q: A CBC in a lavender-top tube is collected on the floor. What is the usual acceptable limit for testing a room-temperature EDTA specimen?
choices: 30 minutes
2 hours only
8 hours only
Within 24 hours, though within a few hours is preferred for accurate cell morphology
questions.why: Routine CBC counts remain acceptable up to about 24 hours at room temperature, but morphology on the smear deteriorates well before then, so prompt testing is preferred. Claiming a hard 30-minute limit confuses CBC with the tighter coagulation rules.

questions.q: A light-blue-top tube is collected for a PTT and is not centrifuged. What is the maximum time to testing?
choices: 1 hour
2 hours
4 hours
24 hours
questions.why: An unspun PTT must be tested within 4 hours because heparin and labile factors degrade quickly. The 24-hour window belongs to the PT, which is the far more stable of the two.

questions.q: Which specimen should NOT be sent through a pneumatic tube system?
choices: A routine CBC in a lavender tube
A specimen for cold agglutinins or one that is hemolysis-sensitive, and any glass or leaking container
A spun chemistry gel tube
A urinalysis in a sealed container
questions.why: Pneumatic tube acceleration and impact cause hemolysis and can break glass or force a leaking container open, and temperature-critical specimens cannot be maintained in transit. Routine spun chemistry and CBC tubes are generally acceptable in a validated system.

questions.q: How should a requisition be transported with its specimen in a biohazard transport bag?
choices: Folded around the tube inside the main compartment
Taped to the outside of the tube
Placed loose in the same compartment as the specimen
In the separate outside pouch of the bag, away from the specimen compartment
questions.why: The paperwork goes in the outer pouch so a leak cannot contaminate or destroy the documentation. Placing it in with the tube risks illegible, biohazardous paperwork if the specimen leaks.

questions.q: A diagnostic blood specimen is being shipped to a reference laboratory by courier. Which classification and packaging applies?
choices: Category B, UN3373, using triple packaging with a leakproof primary receptacle, absorbent material, a leakproof secondary container, and a rigid outer box
Category A, UN2814, single container
No classification is required for patient specimens
Category B, UN1845, double packaging
questions.why: Routine diagnostic specimens are Category B, marked UN3373, and require the triple packaging system. UN2814 is Category A, reserved for substances capable of causing permanent disability or life-threatening disease, and UN1845 is the number for dry ice, not a specimen class.

questions.q: Frozen specimens are being shipped on dry ice. Which statement is correct?
choices: Dry ice should be sealed airtight to prevent sublimation
Dry ice is placed inside the secondary container with the specimen
Dry ice goes outside the secondary container, and the package must allow carbon dioxide gas to vent
Dry ice may be used only for room-temperature specimens
questions.why: Dry ice is a refrigerant placed outside the secondary container, and the outer package must vent sublimating carbon dioxide or it can rupture. An airtight seal is specifically prohibited for this reason.

questions.q: A specimen is to be stored refrigerated. What temperature range applies?
choices: 15 to 30 C
2 to 8 C
-20 C or below
0 to 1 C
questions.why: Refrigerated storage is 2 to 8 C, room temperature is 15 to 30 C, and frozen is -20 C or below. Choosing 15 to 30 C describes ambient storage, not refrigeration.

questions.q: A frozen aliquot has been thawed and refrozen twice while waiting for a send-out run. Why is this a problem?
choices: Repeated freeze-thaw cycles denature proteins and degrade analytes, invalidating results
Repeated freezing concentrates the specimen and raises all values equally
Freeze-thaw cycles only affect the label adhesive
There is no effect as long as the specimen stays below -20 C between thaws
questions.why: Each freeze-thaw cycle damages protein structure and destroys labile analytes, so specimens are aliquoted into single-use portions before freezing. The idea that values simply rise uniformly is false, since the effect is analyte-specific degradation.

questions.q: A light-blue-top coagulation tube arrives with a visible clot. What is the appropriate action?
choices: Break up the clot with an applicator stick and test it
Spin it longer and test the plasma above the clot
Test it and note the clot on the report
Reject the specimen, document the reason, and request recollection
questions.why: A clotted anticoagulated tube has already consumed the clotting factors being measured, so the result is meaningless and the specimen is rejected and documented. Dislodging the clot does not restore the consumed factors and adds hemolysis.

questions.q: Which of the following is NOT a standard specimen rejection criterion?
choices: Grossly hemolyzed serum for a potassium test
A tube filled to its full stated draw volume
Quantity not sufficient for the ordered test
Blood collected in an expired tube
questions.why: A properly filled tube is exactly what is wanted; rejection applies to hemolysis, QNS, expired tubes, clots, wrong tube type, and identification problems. A full tube is only an issue in coagulation if the ratio is off, which is a short-draw problem, not a full-draw one.

questions.q: After rejecting a specimen, what documentation is required?
choices: Nothing, since the specimen was never tested
A verbal note to the next shift
The reason for rejection, the date and time, the person notified, and the notification time, recorded in the LIS or rejection log
Only the accession number crossed off the log
questions.why: Rejection is a reportable preanalytical event that must be documented with reason, time, and who was notified so recollection happens and trends can be tracked. Verbal notification alone leaves no record and no accountability.

questions.q: A blood alcohol specimen is collected for a legal case. What does chain of custody require?
choices: A documented, unbroken record of every person who handled the specimen, with dates, times, and signatures, in a sealed and initialed container
Only that the specimen be labeled and refrigerated
That the specimen be tested in duplicate
That a supervisor draw the specimen
questions.why: Chain of custody is a legal document tracking possession from collection through testing and storage with signatures at each transfer, and the tamper-evident seal is initialed by the collector. Labeling and refrigeration are ordinary handling and do not establish legal custody.

questions.q: A STAT troponin arrives in the laboratory. How should it be handled?
choices: Placed in the routine rack and worked in order of arrival
Given priority handling, logged and processed immediately, with turnaround time tracked from receipt
Held until a batch of chemistry specimens accumulates
Sent to the reference laboratory for faster analysis
questions.why: STAT specimens bypass the routine queue and are processed immediately because the result drives urgent clinical decisions, and turnaround time is a monitored quality indicator. Batching defeats the entire purpose of a STAT order.

questions.q: A patient's hemoglobin today is 14.2 g/dL, but yesterday's value was 8.1 g/dL with no transfusion documented. What quality process flags this?
choices: Levey-Jennings chart
Proficiency testing
Calibration verification
A delta check, which compares a current result to the same patient's previous result
questions.why: A delta check compares consecutive results on the same patient and flags implausible shifts that often signal a mislabeled or switched specimen. Levey-Jennings charts monitor control material over time, not an individual patient's consecutive values.

questions.q: Collecting the specimen, labeling it, and transporting it to the laboratory belong to which phase of testing?
choices: Analytical
Postanalytical
Preanalytical
Interpretive
questions.why: Everything before the instrument runs the sample is preanalytical, and it accounts for the majority of laboratory errors. The analytical phase is the actual measurement, and reporting the result is postanalytical.

questions.q: A critical potassium value of 7.2 mmol/L is called to the nursing unit. What must occur to complete the notification?
choices: The receiver repeats the patient name, test, and value back, and the caller documents the read-back, the time, and the receiver's name
The caller leaves a voicemail and documents the call time
The value is faxed and the fax confirmation is filed
The value is flagged in the LIS for the physician to see at the next login
questions.why: Critical values require direct communication with read-back verification by the receiver, documented with time and name. A voicemail or a passive LIS flag does not confirm that a responsible person actually received and understood the value.

questions.q: A transport bag is opened and the tube inside is cracked and leaking. What is the first action?
choices: Pour the remaining blood into a clean tube and relabel it
Keep the bag closed, don gloves and appropriate PPE, and handle it inside a biological safety cabinet or contained area per policy, then discard and request recollection
Wipe the tube with a paper towel and run the test
Place the bag in the refrigerator until a supervisor arrives
questions.why: A leaking specimen is an exposure hazard, so it is contained with PPE, discarded, and recollected while the incident is documented. Transferring leaked blood to a new tube both risks exposure and produces a specimen of uncertain identity and integrity.

questions.q: A tube broke inside the centrifuge. After the rotor stops and PPE is donned, how is the centrifuge decontaminated?
choices: Rinse the chamber with hot water only
Wipe with alcohol and resume use immediately
Remove glass with forceps or a brush, then disinfect the chamber, cups, and rotor with a 1:10 bleach solution or approved tuberculocidal disinfectant and allow the contact time
Spray with a deodorizer and close the lid
questions.why: Broken glass is never picked up by hand, and the chamber requires an approved disinfectant left for the labeled contact time to be effective. Alcohol wiping alone does not meet the contact time or the tuberculocidal requirement for blood spills.

questions.q: A specimen is received in the laboratory. What does accessioning accomplish?
choices: It establishes the reference range for the test
It replaces the need for a requisition
It substitutes for patient identification at the bedside
It assigns a unique identifying number that links the specimen, the patient, the requisition, and the test order in the LIS, with a documented receipt time
questions.why: Accessioning creates the unique number that ties specimen, patient, and order together and time-stamps receipt for turnaround tracking. It does not replace the requisition or the bedside identification that already established whose blood is in the tube.
